activity: graduating from high school
story:
The gown was too hot before the ceremony even started. Jason stood in the staging area behind the football field bleachers, among two hundred classmates arranged in alphabetical order, waiting for the band to begin. The person beside him, a girl named Priya whom he knew only as the one who beat him in eleventh grade calculus by half a point, was humming under her breath, and it took him a moment to recognize the tune.

"That song," he said. "Do you know where it actually comes from? I've heard it at every graduation since kindergarten and I never once asked."

"Pomp and Circumstance, March Number One," she said. "Edward Elgar. It premiered in 1901, in Liverpool."

He looked at her. "How do you know that?"

"My grandfather played trumpet. He told me the first time I hummed it, which was apparently the same age you were when you started wondering." She said it without smugness, the way his calculus teacher used to say a lemma, a small stepping stone you proved on the way to something larger, and you either knew it or you didn't. Jason had spent four years trying to know things like that. Priya had spent four years knowing them without visible effort.

His phone buzzed in the pocket under his gown. His father: On my way. Traffic on Route 9. He read it twice, then put the phone away. His father had said he was on his way to the regional science fair in tenth grade too, and to the playoff game last spring, and neither time had the arrival actually occurred. There had been a period, after the divorce, when his father claimed to be nearly destitute, and Jason had believed it, and then had seen a photograph of a new truck on his uncle's phone. He didn't know what to do with the contradiction then and he didn't now. He wanted his father in the bleachers. He also wanted to not care whether his father was in the bleachers, and those two wants had been living in him all morning like tenants who refused to speak to each other.

The band started. The sound came across the field thin and slightly late, the way sound did outdoors, and the line began to move. Priya walked ahead of him, alphabet working itself out with perfect indifference to anything either of them had ever done. Jason followed. He thought about the march itself, how something written in 1901 in Liverpool had crossed an ocean and installed itself in every gymnasium and football field in North America, how nobody in the ceremony had chosen it and yet everyone was walking to it. It seemed to him that most of his life so far had that quality. The colleges, the applications, the courses he'd taken because they stacked correctly on a transcript. He had chosen his path the way the school chose its processional music, by inheritance.

He found his chair. The speeches began. The principal enunciated every word carefully, as though the microphone were a stranger she was being formally introduced to, and Jason sat with his hands folded and watched the gate at the far end of the field. A man in a green shirt arrived at the gate and was stopped by an usher, and Jason's whole chest tightened, and then the man turned and it was nobody, some uncle of somebody, and the tightening loosened into something he didn't have a name for.

They called names. Rios. Roberts. When it was his turn he crossed the stage, shook the hand offered to him, took the leather folder, and looked out once at the bleachers, at a blur of hats and sunglasses and small waving hands, and could not tell anything from it. He descended the stairs on the other side and sat down again in the section of chairs reserved for the already-graduated.

Afterward, in the parking lot, gown unzipped, his father was leaning against a car that was not a new truck but not a destitute man's car either. He was holding a grocery-store bouquet, carnations, the kind of thing bought at the last possible minute, and Jason understood that the man had missed the walk itself, the whole processional, Elgar and all, and had arrived in time only for the part where his son already had the folder under his arm. His father raised the flowers slightly, an offering, an apology, an admission, impossible to tell which. Jason stood there holding everything he had decided in the bleachers, that it didn't matter, and everything he had decided on the stage, that it did, and found that he could hold both and still walk.

"You missed the music," Jason said. "It premiered in 1901, in Liverpool."

"Then I'll hum it," his father said, "if you tell me how it goes."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
story:
The parking lot behind the middle school still had the faded cones from summer, and Grayson's grandfather sat in the passenger seat adjusting the mirror as though the mirror were the thing that had to be taught first. "Both hands at nine and three," he said. "And if you ever have to stop fast, pump the brakes. Pump them till you stop. That's how I taught your mother, and she never put a dent in anything I paid for." Grayson nodded, put the car in drive, and let it roll forward over the painted lines while his grandfather hummed something without a melody.

That had been two weeks ago, in the same family sedan his mother was now sliding into the driver's seat of, a driving instructor named Mr. Okafor already waiting by the lot entrance with a clipboard. He was quiet in the way of a man who had spent thirty years watching teenagers discover the width of their own bodies, and he didn't stigmatize the nervous ones, which Grayson appreciated, because his cousin had failed twice and everyone at the dinner table had treated it like a character flaw rather than a bad Tuesday. "You've had some practice," Mr. Okafor said, reading the form. "Ten hours." He handed Grayson the keys. "Show me a left turn out of the lot, then we'll take the road by the canal."

The road by the canal was narrow and tree-dark, and Grayson drove it at the speed of a person carrying something breakable. He thought of his uncle Danny, who called himself a car guy but had never changed his own oil, a dilettante in coveralls, and who had once told Grayson that modern cars did everything for you anyway. His grandfather, on the other hand, was genuinely sagacious about most things, taxes, tomatoes, the temperament of dogs, and yet on this one subject he had been firm. Pump the brakes. Grayson had said nothing at the time, because at sixteen he had said nothing at the time about a lot of things.

They had done lane changes and a three-point turn when Mr. Okafor asked him to pull over and swap seats, and it was while Grayson was checking the mirror for the hundredth unnecessary time that the dog came. It came out of the reeds at the canal edge, low and fast, a brown shape with no collar and total commitment, and it crossed the road maybe four car lengths ahead. Grayson's foot went to the brake the way his grandfather's voice had trained it, and it started to come off, to pump, and then it didn't. He pressed down hard and held it there, and the pedal made a sound like grinding gravel and shuddered against his foot, and while the car was still slowing he turned the wheel, gently, the way you'd turn a doorknob, and the sedan came around the dog with a lane's width to spare and stopped on the shoulder, ticking.

The dog stood in the road, looked at them, and trotted back into the reeds as though it had an appointment. Mr. Okafor's hand, which Grayson now noticed had been hovering near the wheel the whole time, returned to his knee. "You okay?" Grayson said, "yes" before his voice caught, then, "yes," for real. The shuddering in the pedal had frightened him more than the dog had. He sat with his hands at nine and three and asked, because he wanted the man's answer rather than the internet's, "That noise, that's the anti-lock brakes?"

"That's them working," Mr. Okafor said. He looked at Grayson a moment longer. "Where did you learn to do that? Most students pump."

Grayson told him about the parking lot, the cones, the humming. He told him that afterward he had gone home and read the owner's manual cover to cover, which was the kind of thing he did and had decided at some point to stop apologizing for, and that the manual had said to press firmly and hold it, not pump, that these cars had anti-lock brakes and you could keep steering even while braking hard. His grandfather's advice was from a different car, a different decade, given with total confidence. "He wasn't wrong for his car," Grayson said. "He's just still driving it." He heard how that sounded, like a judgment about more than brakes, and let it stand there without deciding whether he meant it.

"He taught you everything else, though," Mr. Okafor said. "Nine and three. Checking the mirror. You did all of that before you touched the brake." He made a note on his clipboard. "Ready to drive back?"

Grayson pulled onto the road. He was thinking that his grandfather would want the whole story tonight, would want to know what the pedal had felt like, and that somewhere in the telling Grayson would have to say that the advice had been out of date, and he did not yet know whether to say it like a correction or like a discovery he happened to have gotten to first. Both might be true. The canal slid past on his side, bright where the sun got through the trees.

At the lot, his mother was leaning against her end of the sedan, phone down, watching them come in. Mr. Okafor got out and said something to her that Grayson couldn't hear, and she laughed, then pressed her hand flat over her mouth the way she did when she was about to cry instead. When Grayson parked and cut the engine, she opened his door before he'd fully stopped moving. "Ten hours," she said. "Your grandfather says four was plenty in his day."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Amy had claimed the good corner of the couch an hour before kickoff, which her brother Danny considered an act of war and which she considered strategy, and now the room was filling up anyway: Danny, their dad, the Nguyens from next door, and Amy's nine-year-old cousin Theo, who arrived carrying a pillow like a shield.

"Giants," Theo announced, "are going to win by a thousand."

"That's not a score anyone can achieve," Danny said, taking the last pretzel.

"It's a vibe," Theo said, and Amy laughed so hard she almost spilled her drink on the remote, which would have ended the game for everyone and made her, briefly, the most hated person in the living room.

The trouble started on a third down in the second quarter. The Giants, down by four, needed six yards, and the yellow line glowed across the field like a strip of raked sunlight. Theo leaned forward, squinting at the screen.

"Why is it yellow?" he asked. "Is it slippery?"

"It's paint," Danny said. "They paint it on the grass."

"They repaint it every first down?" Amy said. "With what, a very fast man and a very long brush?"

Danny shrugged. "Groundskeepers. Professionals."

Amy looked at the line. The camera cut to a sideline shot, then back, and the yellow appeared again, perfectly straight, perfectly placed, following the field like it knew where the sticks were. She thought of her physics teacher, who liked to say that the most rationalism ever achieved by humankind was probably hiding inside a television broadcast, unthanked. If the line were paint, it would smudge when a player slid across it. She had watched receivers slide across it all season. It never smudged.

"Theo," she said, "when the camera zooms in on a player standing on the line, what happens?"

Theo watched. A receiver caught a pass exactly at the yellow stripe, and the camera pushed in tight, and Theo's mouth opened. The yellow wasn't on his shoes. It wasn't on the grass, not really; it was just there, under him and over him and somehow not anywhere at all.

"Whoa," Theo said.

"Whoa what?" their dad said, looking up from his nachos.

"The line's not paint," Theo said. "It's a ghost."

Amy already had her phone out, thumbs moving, because she was the kind of person who could not leave a ghost uninterrogated. She read, and read again, and then held the phone up like a trophy.

"The yellow line is computer-drawn," she said. "It's not on the field at all. It only looks like it is."

"Then where does it come from?" Theo demanded, as if she had personally installed it.

"A company called Sportvision," Amy said, reading. "And get this. The first broadcast with it was ESPN, September 27, 1998."

"That's before I was born," Theo said, in the tone of a man discovering the earth was older than his house.

"That's before Danny was born," Amy said.

"Barely," said Danny, who was twenty and sensitive about it, and the Nguyens' dad said, "Barely is doing a lot of work in that sentence," and the room broke up laughing, even Danny, eventually.

Here was the thing Amy kept turning over while the fourth quarter tightened and everyone shouted at a holding call: she had been wrong about being wrong. She had assumed Danny's explanation was lazy but harmless, the kind of small untruth that underwrites family peace, and instead it had sent Theo believing in magic paint, and it had sent her, for years, never once asking. The lie wasn't deleterious because it hurt anyone; it was deleterious because it was comfortable. She liked knowing things. She liked it less, she was discovering, to notice how many things she'd absorbed without checking, and she could not decide whether that made curiosity a virtue or just a habit with better marketing.

"Ames," Theo whispered, during the two-minute warning, "if the line's not real, is the game real?"

"The game's real," she said. "The line's real too. It's just real somewhere else."

"In the computer?"

"In the computer."

Theo considered this with the seriousness of a philosopher nine years into a hard problem. "So the players can't see it."

"Nope."

"That's so sad. They're just guessing."

"They're not guessing," Danny said. "They have the actual chains on the actual field. The yellow line is for us. We're the ones who needed help."

"A ghost to help us," Theo said, satisfied, and settled back into his pillow.

The Giants drove to the twelve and stalled, and kicked a field goal to tie it, and Theo declared this unacceptable, and Amy found she was smiling at the screen where the yellow stripe lay across the grass like something the world had agreed to pretend. On fourth and one, with eleven seconds left, her dad stood up, blocking the television entirely.

"Dad," everyone said at once.

"Who's thirsty?" he asked, not moving.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
story:
Jasmine had never once been wrong about money, which is why she kept the receipts. She kept them folded in the front pocket of her binder, every Tim Hortons cup and drugstore lip balm, because Ms. Ferreira had said in September that sales tax showed up on receipts whether you looked at it or not. 13 percent in Ontario, blended into the total or listed beneath it, and Jasmine had started seeing it everywhere, a quiet subtraction attached to nearly everything she bought. She was the kind of person who noticed. She told herself she was the kind of person everyone else wished they had around.

The business classroom smelled like dry-erase marker and the radiator's burnt dust. Third period, Grade 12 accounting, and Ms. Ferreira was walking them through a sample paycheque projected on the whiteboard: gross pay, then the deductions carved out of it, income tax withheld, employment insurance, Canada Pension Plan. Net pay sat at the bottom in a smaller, sadder number. "This is not the money you earned," Ferreira said, tapping the gross. "This is the money you get to keep." Danny Kowalski muttered something about robbery, and half the class laughed, and Jasmine didn't, because she was copying the paycheque into her notes with the concentration of someone transcribing scripture.

The unit ended with a field trip to the bank on Ridgeline Avenue, which was really just a walk with permission slips. It was March, refund season, and the branch had put up a curling banner about fast refund deposits. While they waited for the tour to start, Danny stood at the counter beside his older sister, who was cashing her return. When she came back to the cluster of students she was grinning, holding up her phone with the deposit confirmation. "Eighteen hundred bucks," she said. "Free money, baby. Like winning the lottery."

Jasmine felt the correction rise in her before she'd finished deciding whether to say it. "It's not free money, though," she said. "Not extra income either. It's your own money coming back. If you get a refund, it means more was withheld from your pay during the year than you actually owed. It's an overpayment being returned." Danny's sister looked at her the way people look at a red light they didn't want. "Whatever," she said. "It showed up in my account. Felt free to me." Danny excoriated Jasmine all the way back to the school, not cruelly but at volume, calling her the tax police, the receipt girl, asking whether she itemized her birthday cards. She let him. She was right, and being right, she had learned, cost a certain amount of being liked at any given moment.

The part she didn't say out loud, walking back with her hands in her pockets, was the part she wasn't sure about. Her father had been explaining his own return at the kitchen table the night before, forms spread across the counter like a dissection, and he had seemed pleased about his refund too, in a way that suggested she might be missing something. If the money was only ever hers, why did getting it back feel like a windfall to everyone she'd ever met? Maybe there was a whole phylogeny of how people related to their own money, some evolutionary tree of feelings about it, and she occupied a lonely branch. She'd read that word in biology that morning, phylogeny, and liked it, and liked even less admitting that Danny's sister's happiness might be as legitimate as her accuracy.

The following Monday, Ferreira handed back their unit projects. Jasmine's was the paycheque analysis, hers marked ninety-four, with a note in green pen: "Careful with tone when you correct people. Accuracy is not the same as persuasion." She read it four times. She had assumed the note would say something else, something admiring, and for a second she genuinely could not tell whether Ferreira was wrong or whether she was.

At lunch she found Danny's sister outside the bank, back for something, standing near the creek that ran behind the plaza, the riparian strip of dead grass and crushed reeds marking where the water rose in spring. Jasmine had her binder with her, receipts still in the pocket, though she wasn't sure anymore what she planned to do with them. "Hey," she said. "I wasn't trying to ruin it. The eighteen hundred." Danny's sister shrugged, scrolling her phone. "You didn't ruin it. I already spent it." Then, pocketing the phone, she said, "You know what I mean, though. All year it's gone, gone, gone, and then one day it comes back."

Jasmine looked at the creek, at the grey water moving under the last of the ice, and didn't answer, because both things were true and she couldn't yet say how. Danny's sister started walking toward the bus stop, and Jasmine stood a moment longer, then opened the binder and smoothed one receipt flat against her knee, the sales tax printed small at the bottom, and put it back.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
story:
Vincent had forty-one tabs open, but only one mattered. It was the dashboard his school had rolled out that September: every student's name in a column, and beside each name a number that shifted, sometimes hourly, according to how the district's new system scored their behavior on school accounts. The system watched logins, typing cadence, flagged words in email drafts, even how long a cursor idled over a page before scrolling. Vincent's number had dropped eleven points since Friday, and he could not find out why.

He clicked through the FAQ, which offered nothing but reassurance phrased like a legal disclaimer. The system, it said, promoted "digital citizenship." It did not say who had written the rules it enforced, or why Marisol, who typed slowly because of a wrist injury, sat near the bottom of his class while Ryan, who never wrote anything at all, sat at the top. Vincent had noticed that pattern three weeks ago and had not been able to stop noticing it since, the way you can't stop feeling a loose tooth.

His brother Theo was home from his first semester abroad, sprawled on the bed with a sullen expression that had something to do with a girl named Anouk. Vincent swiveled his chair. "Does your school rank you? Like, score you for what you do online?"

Theo looked up. "They tried, actually. First week. There was a whole thing about it."

"A whole thing how?"

"Someone printed the law and taped it to the rector's door." Theo sat up, pulled out his phone, and after a minute of scrolling read aloud: "The European Union's AI Act. It entered into force on August 1, 2024. It bans some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people."

Vincent turned back to his screen and typed those words into the search bar, half expecting them to dissolve into vagueness. They didn't. The regulation was real, the date was real, and somewhere in its articles was a list of prohibited practices, and ranking people by their behavior with automated systems was on it. Bans some uses of AI outright. He read the phrase four times. In Europe, what his school was doing to him every day wasn't a policy debate. It was simply illegal.

"It doesn't help me," he said, almost to himself. "I don't live there."

"No," Theo said. "But it means somebody already had this argument, and somebody already won it." He flopped back down, then added, "Anouk was one of the ones who taped the pages up. She's very..."

Vincent wasn't listening anymore. He had opened a blank document and begun drafting an email to the school board. He wrote two furious paragraphs, deleted them, and started over. His father, who worked in logistics and had watched a warehouse he managed for nine years automate itself down to a skeleton crew, had tried for years to inculcate in his sons a certain wariness toward systems that make decisions no human can be asked to account for. Vincent had always nodded and half-listened. Now he was quoting regulations with citations, and he could almost hear his father's voice behind his own typing.

The draft was going well until he remembered Ryan. Ryan, who never wrote anything, whose silence the system read as virtue. If the board scrapped the scores tomorrow, Ryan would lose his place at the top of a list that had never measured anything, and Ryan's mother, who mentioned the number at every parent night, would lose it too. Vincent sat with that. He had wanted the system gone because it was unfair to him and to Marisol, and it was also, in a smaller and stranger way, the only thing Ryan had ever been good at.

He cut the email down to one page. He kept the citation, the date, the words social scoring, and the question of whether the district's lawyers had considered it. He ended with a request to appear at the next public meeting, and then, before he could think better of it, he sent it.

At the meeting two weeks later, a lawyer for the district explained that the regulation Vincent had cited governed Europe, and this was Ohio, and the district's counsel had reviewed the system and found it compliant with all applicable law. She said "applicable" the way people say a word they've been briefed on. Vincent, sitting in the third row with Theo's printout folded in his pocket, asked whether the board believed the practice was right, not merely legal, and the room went quiet in the particular way rooms go quiet when a question has landed somewhere no one wants to look.

The board voted to form a review committee, which everyone understood to mean nothing would change this year, or probably next. Walking out through the parking lot, Vincent saw Marisol by the chain-link fence, holding her phone up to show her mother the number on the screen, both of them squinting at it in the cold light. "I could ask for clemency," Marisol said dryly, when she noticed him. "There's a form." She laughed, and Vincent laughed, and then neither of them said anything, and the doors of the building swung shut behind the last of the board members, one of whom paused on the steps to look back at them.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
story:
The odometer turned over some number Alexandra would never remember, and she watched the guardrails flick past like frames of a film she hadn't chosen. Three weeks into the new school, and she still rode to school with her mother, because the bus route was a forty-minute loop and because riding with her mother meant twenty more minutes of not being the new girl in a room. She held her phone low in her lap, thumbing back through the thread from Priya and Noor, which had gone from pages of prolix joking to a few lines a day, then to photographs of a lunch table she wasn't at. She was trying to work out whether friendship faded at a steady rate or all at once, the way ice does.

"It's the red barn," her mother said, taking the turn toward the school. "You can tell you're close when you see the red barn."

"I know, Mom." She did know. She had learned the route the way you learn anything you repeat, without wanting to, and she was beginning to suspect that was how the new town would come into her too, grain by grain, whether she consented or not.

In study hall she had found a number that had been bothering her ever since. She'd been scrolling, half-reading an article about how people make friends, and there it was: a 2018 study by a communication researcher named Jeffrey Hall estimating that it takes roughly fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Fifty hours. She had done the arithmetic on the back of her chem notes, embarrassed by herself for doing arithmetic at all. She and Priya had logged that in a single September once, weekends and bus rides and the night they watched three movies in a row. But Dana, who sat beside her in English and lent her a pen and laughed once, genuinely, at something Alexandra said about the Odyssey, how many hours was that? Six? Seven? It was like standing at the bottom of a staircase and being told how tall the building was.

The problem wasn't the number. The problem was what to do with it. One part of her wanted to treat it like a machine you could feed: sit near Dana at lunch, join the literary magazine, bank the hours, wait. Another part said that was exactly wrong, that friendship constructed on a schedule wasn't friendship but a simulation of it, something closer to a transaction. In English they had started a unit on existentialism, and Mr. Reyes kept saying that essence precedes existence or was it the reverse, and Alexandra had written in her margin, does it count if you choose it on purpose? She didn't know. She was good at not knowing lately; she had a lot of practice.

Her mother noticed things in her own way, from the driver's seat, where Alexandra thought of her as scenery with opinions. In the third week of the drive, she had watched her daughter in the mirror, hunched over the phone, and she recognized the posture from her own first year at the hospital, when she had been transferred and nobody had known her name. She had never told Alexandra that. She had instead sublimated the whole thing into casseroles, into joining the neighborhood association, into learning people's dog's names before their own, and it had worked, mostly, though she could not have said whether it had worked because it was a good plan or because time passes regardless.

That Friday, Alexandra asked before the red barn appeared. "Can Dana come over Saturday? Her mom can drop her at the Sheetz."

Her mother kept her eyes on the road so as not to ruin it. "All afternoon?"

"Until dinner. Maybe after." Alexandra looked out the window. "It's not like we're already friends. It's more like we're becoming friends. There's a study. Fifty hours, roughly, to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. That's all a casual friend is, just the hours. Nobody tells you that part."

"Fifty hours," her mother repeated, as if tasting it. "And how many do you have?"

"Seven. Maybe eight." The barn slid past, red and leaning, and Alexandra turned in her seat to keep it in view. "So Saturday's, like, five. If she stays till nine."

Her mother smiled at the windshield and said nothing about the arithmetic, because some things you let a person keep private even when you can see them plainly.

Saturday came cold and bright. Dana arrived at two with a bag of sour candies and a paperback of poems so annotated it looked vandalized, and they sat on the porch steps arguing about which of them was more pretentious, and when Alexandra's phone buzzed with a photo from Priya, the lunch table again, someone's face mid-laugh, she looked at it for a long moment and then set it face down on the step beside her. Dana was reading a line aloud, twice, the way you do when a sentence deserves it, and Alexandra leaned over to see the page.

story:
The admissions table for the business school had run out of brochures by noon, and Jake had been standing behind it for three hours, refilling a bowl of mints nobody touched. He had signed up to volunteer at the university open house mostly because his mother said it would look good on an application he had already submitted, which struck him now, watching a tour group drift past without slowing, as a strange kind of deferred reasoning. He wanted, more concretely, to get out of the tent for twenty minutes.

He found Marcus on the quad steps, holding a phone in both hands and frowning at it with the particular calm of someone who has decided not to care. Marcus was a year older, deferred a semester, working at his uncle's moving company, and he had driven Jake here because Jake's mother worked Saturdays.

"I missed a payment," Marcus said, before Jake could sit down. "On the card. They sent a thing."

"How bad?"

"They charged me a fee. Forty bucks. It's paid now." He shrugged, blasé in the way he got about money, as though numbers were weather, something that happened to you. "Whatever, it's one payment."

A girl coming down the steps with a lanyard and a clipboard overheard him. She slowed, seemed to debate with herself, then stopped. "Sorry. Are you talking about a credit card?" She had a volunteer badge like Jake's, from the financial literacy table two tents over. "Because my brother did that. Missed one payment, figured it was done once he paid the fee. It stayed on his credit report for seven years."

"Seven," Marcus repeated.

"Most negative stuff, late payments, that kind of thing, seven years," she said. "Bankruptcies are worse. Up to ten." She hitched the clipboard higher. "He found out when he tried to get an apartment at twenty-six. Anyway. Sorry for eavesdropping." She went on toward the fountain, already scanning the crowd for her table partner, who was probably drowning in visitors.

Marcus looked at the phone again. He was quiet for a moment, and Jake watched him do the arithmetic that Jake was doing himself: seven years from now Marcus would be twenty-five. Out of his uncle's van, presumably. Applying for something. A lease, a loan, a life that required strangers to trust a file with his name on it.

"That's a long time," Marcus said.

"It's not a prison sentence," Jake said. "It's a mark."

"A mark for seven years because I forgot to pay eighty dollars."

The girl was walking back now, and Jake thought she was coming to soften what she'd said, but she was carrying two cups from the lemonade stand and handed one to Marcus, who took it like it settled something. "I'm Priya, by the way," she said. "My brother's fine now, if that helps. He got the apartment eventually. It's not the end of the world, it's just, it follows you. Longer than you'd think."

"Everything at this thing follows you," Jake said. "That's the whole pitch." He gestured at the tents, the tours, the banners with the school's motto in a font that implied permanence. "Choose your major, choose your dorm, choose your future. Nobody says choose your Saturday volunteer shift because it might matter in a decade, but my mom did, and here I am."

Marcus laughed for the first time that afternoon. Priya did too, then grew serious in a way that made Jake straighten up. "Can I ask you something? You're applying here, right? Business?" He nodded. "I'm doing finance, and everyone at my table keeps asking what you actually do with it, and I keep giving the same answer, advising people on their money, and my dad says that's not a job description, that's a mood." She looked at the fountain. "I want to be a fiduciary. Someone who has to put the client's interest first, actually has to, by law. My dad's advisor wasn't one, and my dad lost a lot in a deal where the guy got paid either way. Nobody indemnified us for any of it, nobody made it right. So." She stopped, embarrassed, as if she'd said more than she meant to.

"That's a real answer," Jake said. "That's more than a mood."

Marcus turned his cup in his hands. "So you'd tell people like me the seven years thing before I missed the payment."

"That's the idea," Priya said.

They sat with that, the three of them, while another tour group filed past, a guide walking backward and promising that the library was open twenty-four hours during finals. Marcus set up an autopay on his phone right there on the steps, thumbing through it slowly, reading each screen, which he never did. Then he said he should get the car warmed up for the drive home, though the open house had two hours left, and Jake understood that Marcus wanted to go tell his uncle, or maybe just be alone with the arithmetic.

Jake stayed until his shift ended, then walked past the financial literacy table on his way out. Priya was handing a worksheet to a father and son, and she caught his eye and raised the lemonade cup an inch. He thought about his own file, wherever it was, already accumulating marks he couldn't see yet, applications submitted, choices logged, this Saturday among them. He couldn't decide whether that was terrifying or comforting, whether it was better to be watched by the future or simply to owe it something.

At the parking lot, Marcus had the window down, elbow out, radio low. "Hey," he said as Jake got in. "Seven years from now, if I'm buying a house or whatever, remind me of today."

"I'll put it on your credit report," Jake said, and pulled the door shut.

story:
Keira found her grandmother's recipe box open on the counter, as if it had been waiting, and decided that tonight she would make the lemon cake her mother had written onto an index card years ago. The kitchen smelled of the rosemary her grandmother kept drying over the window, and the late sun laid long stripes across the tile. Keira's grandmother was in the garden pulling the last of the beans, and her little brother, Dane, sat at the table drawing spaceships, so the kitchen was Keira's for the hour before their parents drove up from the city.

She had texted her mother a photo of the card, and her mother had replied with a message Keira read aloud to Dane: "That recipe! Your grandma used to make it every August. Don't skimp on the zest. Love you both." Below that, a second message: "There's a farmers market two blocks from her house if you need anything. Wish I was here." Keira set the phone face-up where she could see it and began.

She creamed the butter and sugar the way the card instructed, humming a little, feeling capable and grown. She zested two lemons until her wrist ached, added the juice, folded in the flour in three careful additions. The batter looked like something from a photograph. Then she reached the line that said three eggs, one at a time, and opened the refrigerator.

There were no eggs. There was a jar of pickles, half an onion in cling film, and a carton of oat milk her grandmother bought for coffee. Keira stood with the door open until the cold touched her face, then checked the pantry, the garage fridge that hummed like a sleeping animal, even the blue cooler on the back porch. Nothing. The clock over the stove gave her forty minutes before her parents arrived, and the market closed in twenty-five.

She called into the garden. "Grandma, did you use all the eggs?"

Her grandmother straightened up slowly, one hand at the small of her back. "I made a frittata for the neighbors Tuesday. I keep forgetting to buy more. I don't bake much anymore, sweetheart."

"I'm halfway through a cake. Mom's recipe."

Her grandmother came inside, washed her hands, and looked at the bowl with real interest, not the polite kind. "You measured everything before you started?"

"Flour, sugar, lemons. Not eggs. Obviously."

"Mise en place," her grandmother said. "Everything in its place, measured out before you begin. Your grandfather teased me about it for fifty years, all my little dishes." She touched the batter with one fingertip and tasted it. "You'll know for next time."

Keira looked at the bowl of beautiful, eggless batter, at Dane still drawing, at the fading light. Part of her wanted to say it wasn't fair, that the recipe was old and had ambushed her, but she was sixteen and could walk two blocks, and she said so. "Market closes at six. I can run it."

"Wear the yellow jacket," her grandmother said, already reaching for her keys. "And take Dane. He needs the walk more than the eggs do."

They ran the two blocks together, Dane narrating the spaceships the whole way, and Keira felt almost sanguine about the whole thing, the crisis softened by the simple fact that it had a solution. At the market a woman with a table of brown eggs was packing up but sold Keira a half dozen and refused to charge her for the carton. "From one baker to another," the woman said, and Keira thanked her twice because she could not tell whether the second thank you or the first had been the sincere one.

Back in the kitchen, her grandmother had not touched the batter. She had, however, set out six small dishes along the counter, each holding a measured something for tomorrow morning's breakfast: flour, milk, a spoon of oil, and an empty dish waiting for the eggs. She said nothing about it, and Keira said nothing either, but she saw it.

She cracked the three eggs into the batter one at a time, watching each disappear into the yellow, and slid the pan into the oven while Dane pressed his nose to the glass. When her parents came through the door, the smell reached the hallway before the greetings did, and her mother found the index card on the counter, thumb-worn and butter-stained now, and held it up without saying anything at all.

Keira wrote on the back of the card, in small letters under her mother's handwriting: mise en place. Then she set the table.

story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and cold air, and Evan stood in the line for the teller holding his paycheque from Hannaford's like it might tear. He had two of them crumpled together, four weeks of bagging groceries, and on the stub of the newer one he could read the arithmetic that had been quietly adjudicating his life all summer: gross pay, then federal income tax withheld, then a state line, then something called FICA that nobody had ever explained to him. The cheque itself was for the smaller number, the one left over after the deductions had taken their share, and he had folded it into his pocket so many times the ink had gone soft along the crease.

The problem was the refund, or rather the absence of one. His mother had left a note on the kitchen table that morning, her handwriting leaning hard to the right as it always did when she was tired: "Tax deadline is Tuesday. If you don't file you lose the money they took out, and we need it for the car. Love, Mom." She worked nights at the hospital and slept days, so the note was their whole conversation. He had done the return himself on the library computer, following the form line by line, income here, withholding there, and the software kept insisting he was owed three hundred and forty dollars, which was the difference between the car getting its alternator replaced and Evan riding his bike eleven miles to work through November.

He reached the teller, a woman named Dolores whose badge said she'd been there longer than Evan had been alive. "Deposit, and I need to know when the refund comes," he said. She looked at the cheque, then at him, then at the stub he'd flattened against the counter so she could see the withholding. "Direct deposit on the return, sweetheart, if you gave them your account number. Otherwise a cheque in the mail, couple weeks maybe." He had given them the account number, this account, the one with $61.13 in it. "Tuesday's the deadline," he said. "If I filed yesterday." She smiled at the ceiling. "Then you're fine, and the government is slower than me even on my worst day."

Behind him a toddler had become obstreperous, throwing a sippy cup against the velvet rope while her father apologized to the entire room, and Evan stepped aside to fill out his slip at the little desk with the chained pen. That was where Marcus found him, still in his gas station uniform, holding a receipt and frowning at it like it had insulted his mother.

"Okay, so explain this," Marcus said, laying two receipts side by side on the desk. Both were for the same thing, a Monster energy drink and a bag of jalapeño chips, bought within an hour of each other last Saturday on their drive up to the lake. "Same stuff, same price on the shelf. Look at the totals." Evan looked. One receipt came to $5.83. The other came to $5.67. At the bottom of each, under the items, a line for tax: thirty-one cents on one, fifteen on the other.

"We didn't even go that far," Marcus said. "Crossed the county line, that's it. Rhinebeck to Red Hook." He said the word "oligarchy" then, the way he'd been saying it all summer since his brother got political, some theory that the towns with the big houses quietly arranged things so the towns without them paid more. "Sixteen cents," Marcus said. "Somebody decided that."

Evan copied the numbers onto the back of his deposit slip and stared at them. He thought about his paycheque, how the federal government took its income tax off the top, one rate everywhere, printed right there on the stub. But the sales tax wasn't like that. There was no national one, he realized, working it through out loud: sales taxes were set by states and local governments, so the rate on a receipt depended on where you happened to be standing when you bought the chips. Same drink, same shelf price, two different towns, two different taxes. "It's not Rhinebeck deciding to stick it to us," Evan said slowly. "It's just that nobody in Washington sets this one. Each place sets its own."

"Then move the lake party to Red Hook," Marcus said, and Evan laughed, though he kept the receipts, folding them into his wallet next to the paycheque stubs. Both were records of the same quiet transaction, he thought: money leaving him, itemized, one taken before he ever touched it and one added at the counter, and only one of which he could vote on locally, or avoid by driving four miles out of his way.

He handed Dolores the slip and the cheque. She counted nothing, tapped keys, and told him the balance would be $61.13 plus $412.88 until the refund landed. "Alternator money," Evan said, mostly to himself. "Alternator money," Dolores agreed, stamping the deposit with a thump of her rubber stamp, and behind them the toddler hurled the sippy cup again.

story:
Brody set his phone face down beside his plate before his mother could say anything about it, which was itself a kind of announcement. Across the table his father was already halfway through the story of the drive home, how he'd started the trip on the classic rock station out of Hartwell and finished it, two hours later, listening to the exact same afternoon host on the exact same station in Kesterson. "Same guy, same bits, same traffic report," his father said, sawing at his pork chop. "Even read the same weather like it was live."

"Maybe it was recorded," his mother offered.

"Two different cities, two different call letters, and the man says, right here in Kesterson, it's seventy-one and sunny. It was raining, Brody. You could see it was raining." His father laughed, but Brody didn't, because something about it snagged. Last summer, at his grandmother's place three states away, he'd turned on the radio and heard a voice he knew, the sycophant from the morning show back home who laughed at everything the host said even when it wasn't a joke. He'd assumed then that he'd found some syndicated program, the way the same sitcom runs in every market, and he'd let it go. Tonight, watching his father's fork circle the plate, he wanted to know how far it went.

He picked the phone back up. His mother raised an eyebrow; he said, "Thirty seconds," and meant it. He searched the Hartwell station and the Kesterson station and found they weren't cousins or partners but the same company, one owner listed for both, and for four more stations in between. Then he searched how that could be legal, and the answer came up fast, from a trade publication, not a textbook: the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which had eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership. After that, the number of station owners in the country fell sharply, even as the number of stations kept growing.

"There's no cap anymore," he said, mostly to the table. "There used to be a national cap on how many radio stations one company could own. Ninety-six. They got rid of it."

"Ninety-six the year or ninety-six the number?" his father asked, and Brody had to admit he hadn't checked which, only that the law was from 1996 and the cap was national and it was gone. His mother said the same thing had happened to newspapers, more or less, though she said it carefully, the way she said things when she was circling something else.

Brody cogitated on that while he ate. He'd been arguing all week in his civics class about whether the news could be trusted, and he'd taken the loud position, the one that felt good in a room full of people his age: that the media was monolithic and corrupt and obviously so. He'd enjoyed saying it. Now the turbid feeling in his head was different, because the evening host his father liked, the one who gave away concert tickets and remembered callers by name, worked for the same company as the sycophant, and neither of them had chosen that, and the tickets were real, and the weather report was mostly right. It wasn't a conspiracy. It was a purchase.

"Wait," he said, and put the phone flat on the table between the salt and the green beans. He'd clicked through to the article his civics class had read two weeks ago, the one about media consolidation that he'd waved around as proof of everything. The byline was a real reporter. The publication was owned, according to the site's own footer, by a company that also owned six radio stations. He turned the screen toward his father. "Even the story about it is owned by somebody."

His father leaned in, chewing slower. His mother said, quietly, "Your grandfather sold his print shop the same year, remember. He said it was either sell or watch it die." Nobody had ever told Brody the buyer's name before tonight, and his father didn't say it now either; he just pushed his plate an inch toward the center of the table and said, "So who do you believe, then?"

Brody looked at the rain starting against the window, seventy-one and sunny somewhere in Kesterson, and said, "I don't know yet." His father reached over and turned the phone back face down, gently, like closing a book he wasn't finished with.

story:
The tassel kept hitting David in the eye, which he took as a sign. He stood in the corner of the parking lot where the graduates had been herded after the ceremony, holding the maroon folder the principal had pressed into his hands, and he could not make himself open it. Around him, classmates were hugging and shouting phone numbers across the asphalt, which already smelled of hot tar and someone's spilled fruit punch.

"You're staring at it like it's a snake," said Priya, drifting over with her cap tilted back. Her own folder was tucked under her arm like a baguette. Priya had wanted all spring to be voted Most Likely to Be Remembered, a superlative that had gone, absurdly, to a boy who mostly slept in the back of AP Gov. She had campaigned for it with posters. Actual posters.

"I'm savoring," David said. "Savoring takes time."

"You've been savoring for ten minutes. My grandmother's waiting and she thinks a podium fell on you."

He opened it. Inside, on fake velvet, lay the diploma, flat and slightly glossy, his name printed in a font that reminded him of a restaurant menu. "Huh," he said. "It's not even folded."

"What?"

"The thing. The word diploma. It comes from a Greek word meaning paper folded double, because they used to fold official documents." He turned the paper over, as though a crease might be hiding on the back. "This one is unfolded. They didn't even try."

Priya squinted at him. "How do you know that?"

"Mr. Alvarez said it in homeroom in like October, and everyone was asleep, and it stuck in my head like a piece of gum. I've been carrying it around for months with nowhere to put it." He felt oddly pleased and oddly cheated at once, which was a combination he was starting to recognize as the house style of being eighteen.

Priya plucked the diploma out of his hands and folded it in half, briskly, the way you'd fold a map. "There. Now it's historically accurate."

"Now it's creased. That's different. Folding double was a whole practice, an official thing. This is just vandalism." He took it back and attempted to smooth the fold, which of course made it worse, leaving a pale stripe across his name. David Al-Farsi, bisected.

"My grandmother folded everything," Priya said. "Letters, money, her samosas. She says you can tell what someone values by how they fold it." She checked the parking lot, then leaned in. "Also, I need a favor. The yearbook staff left a box of the superlative certificates in the trunk of Ms. Ho's car, and I may have taken mine. The one that says Most School Spirit, which I did not win, but which had my name on it because of a printing error, so philosophically it's mine."

David laughed, a real one that startled him. "Philosophically."

"It's a tenable position. It has my name. It's a certificate of me."

"It's a certificate of someone's typo."

"Semantics." She said it grandly, like a word that ended arguments. Her grandmother honked from the far row, a short impatient blast, and Priya raised a hand without turning.

A boy named Marcus wandered past with his gown unzipped to the waist, dragging it like a cape, and cajoled a freshman into taking a photo of him "looking contemplative" against the flagpole. The freshman took eleven photos, all of them blurry, and Marcus thanked him with the sincerity of a senator. Somewhere a car door slammed and someone's aunt was shouting about a restaurant reservation.

"Here's what I can't decide," David said, watching Marcus pose. "My dad wants me to study engineering because it's practical. My mom keeps saying do what you love, which is history, and everyone treats that like she suggested juggling. And I keep thinking the diploma thing proves both of them wrong. It's a folded piece of paper that isn't even folded anymore, and everyone still treats it like it's the most important object I'll ever hold." He weighed the folder in his hand. "So either the folding mattered and we forgot, or it never mattered and we remember wrong. And I genuinely don't know which one's scarier."

Priya considered this with the seriousness she usually reserved for her own campaigns. "Or," she said, "the folding mattered, and then it stopped mattering, and the word just kept going because people like having a thing to hand each other." She took her own folder out from under her arm and looked at it for the first time all day. "That's actually kind of nice. The word outlived the reason."

"That's not nice. That's terrifying."

"Fine, it's both. You're allowed to have it be both, that's what the grown-ups never tell you." Her grandmother honked again, twice, and Priya sighed and jammed her cap more firmly onto her head. "Coming, Ammachi!"

She made it three steps, then turned and walked backward, shouting across the asphalt: "Fold it once more before you frame it! Double folded! For the ancestors!"

David looked down at the diploma, at the crease running through his name, at the flat glossy paper in its velvet cradle. He folded it once, precisely, along Priya's line, and held it up to the sun so the light came through both halves at once.

story:
Gabrielle had been carrying the same manila folder to the community art studio every Tuesday for six weeks, and it still held only four finished pieces. She arranged them on the long table by the window: two watercolors of her grandmother's hands, a charcoal study of the kitchen faucet that dripped all summer, and a print she had made of the sink itself, its basin crowded with drowned moths. The theme was supposed to be hands and water, or maybe just things that repeat, and she had promised herself, and Ms. Okafor at the studio, that by spring she would have ten pieces ready. Ten felt like a real number, solid and countable, the kind of thing you could hold up to a magistrate and say, here, this is a body of work.

The studio smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee. On Tuesdays it filled with retirees painting orchards and a few teenagers who came because school art was only forty minutes and a shared sink. Marcus was there already, a senior from the public school across town, truculent as always about the drying racks, which someone had reorganized overnight into an order he did not respect.

"That's mine," he said, pulling a canvas off the rack before Gabrielle had even unpacked her brushes. "Somebody moved it into the wrong slot."

"Everything got moved. They cleaned." She watched him set the canvas down with exaggerated care, and then, because she wanted to talk to someone other than her own folder, she said, "Can I ask you something about AP Art? You took it last year, right?"

"2-D Art and Design." He said it the way people name a rival they respect. "Why."

"I'm building a portfolio. Ten pieces on one theme, plus a statement. Ms. Okafor's making me write the statement first, before I even finish." Gabrielle turned one of the watercolors toward him, the close-up of her grandmother's knuckles wrapped around a wet dish towel. "But I don't actually know what schools want."

Marcus looked at the watercolor for longer than she expected. "Ten pieces is a gallery thing," he said. "The AP portfolio isn't ten." He wiped his hands on his jeans. "The Sustained Investigation section asks for fifteen digital images. And it counts for sixty percent of your score."

"Sixty percent of the whole score?"

"That section, yeah. Fifteen images." He shrugged, as if he had delivered bad news often enough that the delivery no longer interested him. "People fail it because they make nine good pieces and then sprint in April."

Gabrielle sat down on the paint-spattered stool and did the arithmetic in her notebook, twice, because the first time the numbers seemed truculent themselves. Ten pieces became fifteen images only if every piece photographed into one image, which they wouldn't, since process shots counted, since sketchbook pages counted, since the investigation itself, the questions she was asking, had to show its own thinking. Her theme, things that repeat, was suddenly not a folder but a corridor, and it was longer than she had measured.

She worked that Tuesday without talking much. She photographed the four finished pieces from three angles each, and then, on impulse, photographed her own hands photographing them, which made her laugh out loud at the copying table and embarrassed her into silence. At home she opened a blank document and titled it Artist's Statement, which Ms. Okafor had wanted all along, and Gabrielle had resisted because writing about the work felt like explaining a joke. Now she understood it differently, not as explanation but as a map for where she still had to go. She typed: My grandmother's hands repeat the same motions her mother's did, over the same sink, in a house that no longer exists. What is inherited, and what is just worn in?

The next Tuesday she brought the statement to the studio and read it aloud to Ms. Okafor, who listened with her arms folded and then said, "Good. Now make me five more pieces that argue with it." Gabrielle spent the evening sketching the well outside her grandmother's old house in Opelousas, which she had visited exactly once, and a series of faucets from the studio bathroom, and her own hands doing nothing at all, resting, which was the hardest thing she had ever tried to draw honestly.

She did not tell her mother that the plan had grown from ten pieces to fifteen images, because her mother would have heard it as more time, more Saturdays in Opelousas, more of the money set aside for the studio's sliding-scale fees. Some of that was true. Gabrielle kept the older number in her head anyway, ten, like a first draft she could not quite delete, and let the two figures sit side by side without reconciling them. What she knew for certain was narrower than what she had believed she knew in September: that the portfolio had a shape, that the shape was partly hers and partly not, and that the part that was not hers was not therefore an enemy. The requirement had not crushed her investigation; it had invigorated it, stretched it like a spine, though she could not yet say whether the stretch would strengthen it or simply make it thinner.

In April there were fourteen images in her folder and a fifteenth half-drawn, the resting hands, still not right. Marcus had graduated and stopped coming. Ms. Okafor stood over the drying rack at closing time while Gabrielle pinned up the newest piece, a watercolor of the studio sink with her brushes soaking in it, and said nothing for a long moment.

"That one's the truest," Ms. Okafor said finally. "The hands are wrong, though."

"I know," Gabrielle said, and unclipped it, and carried it back to the table while the lights were still on.

story:
Cameron sat on the screened porch of his grandmother's house with a block of basswood in his lap and a gouge in his right hand, shaving curls toward the floor. The printout of a wren lay pinned beside him on the table, its feathers translated into a grid of cuts. He had promised her a carving before he left for college, nine days from now, and he had promised himself it would be good, which was a different and heavier promise.

His cousin Dez, ten years old, had been watching from the doorway for most of an hour, chewing the eraser end of a yellow pencil. Now she had worked her way down to the other end. She bit the wood, made a face, and kept chewing.

"Stop that," Cameron said. "You're eating varnish."

"I always chew them." She came and sat on the step below him, holding the pencil out like evidence. Something had flaked off the yellow paint onto her tongue. "Wait. Is this the lead kind? Mr. Rowley said lead makes you sick. Like your brain. Tyler's brother said a kid died from eating a pencil."

Cameron looked at the mangled pencil, and then at the ceiling of the porch, where his thoughts tended to go when they were assembling themselves. He had spent a whole unit on toxicology in chemistry, and it occurred to him that he had never actually checked what was inside a pencil, only repeated what everyone said. He turned it over. "Okay. It's called lead, but that's the wrong word for it."

"So I ate lead."

"You didn't." He held up his own pencil, unsharpened, and tapped the gray tip. "The name goes back to the 1500s. When they found graphite, they thought it was a kind of lead ore. So they called it lead, and everybody kept calling it that. It was never the metal."

Dez squinted at him, deciding whether he was messing with her. "Then what is it?"

"Graphite. Carbon." He thought of the periodic table poster in his room at home, the same column as diamond, which he found beautiful in a way he had never said out loud to anyone. "It's just carbon. Like charcoal. Like basically pencil shavings."

She ran her tongue over her teeth anyway, suspicious. "Then why do they still say lead if it's wrong?"

"Because names stick even after they're wrong." As soon as he said it he understood that he meant more than pencils, though he couldn't have said exactly what. He set down the gouge and picked up the pencil again, turning it in the light, the cheap paint catching sun. A thing could be carrying a lie and still be ordinary, harmless, sitting in every desk in the country.

His grandmother came out with two glasses of lemonade and a dish towel over her shoulder, and she was effusive about the wren's half-emerged wing, the way she was effusive about everything he made, which he both wanted and did not trust. "That's better than the duck," she said. "The duck looked like it had been through something."

"The duck had been through something."

"Well, then it was honest." She set the glasses down and stayed standing, which meant she was working up to a request. "Dez, sweetheart, tell him what you told me this morning."

Dez went still in the way she did before big asks. "I want you to teach me. Carving. Before you go." She said it flat, without the pleading that would have made it easy to refuse. "I saved forty dollars from mowing. I'll pay for wood."

Cameron looked at his remaining nine days, which he had already budgeted in his head: two for packing, one for Marcus's goodbye party, and the rest, secretly, for this porch and this block of wood. "You don't have to pay me."

"I want to pay for the wood. I'm not a charity." Her chin was set the way their grandfather's used to set, in family photographs from before either of them was born.

He thought about his father, who called him an ideologue last spring when he'd argued too hard at dinner about art schools versus real degrees, and how the word had stung mostly because it was half true. He had principles about teaching, about not doing it for money, about what an apprenticeship was supposed to be. He also had a cousin with forty dollars in an envelope, and forty dollars meant something to her that it didn't mean to him. Maybe both things could be true at once and he could stand in the middle of them, holding neither perfectly.

"Fine. You buy the wood," he said. "I keep the money thing out of it, that's my one rule. And we start with graphite, not knives. Drawing before cutting."

Dez stood up so fast the lemonade sloshed. "Can we go to the hardware store now? Grandmother, can he drive your car?"

His grandmother held out the keys without comment, but her eyebrows did something complicated, and Cameron understood that she had been on Dez's side the whole time, that the lemonade had been strategy. He took the keys. On his way to the door he noticed he was still carrying his own pencil, and he turned back for the gouge, out of habit, out of some new instinct about which tools mattered.

In the car Dez rolled the mangled yellow pencil between her fingers, then held it out to him. "Keep this," she said. "So you remember to tell the next kid."

He put it behind his ear and backed down the gravel drive, the wren unfinished on the porch behind them, its wing half raised, waiting exactly where he had left it.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Natalie was the last one through the gym doors, carrying the cooler of sodas her mother had iced at noon. The end-of-season party was Coach Okafor's idea, held on the court itself because nobody wanted to rent a room, and the seniors had claimed the bleachers near the far basket, where the afternoon light came through the high windows in dusty columns. Natalie set the cooler under the scorer's table and looked at the five of them up there, the seniors, in their warm-up jackets with the sleeves pushed to the elbows, and understood with a small physical jolt that the roster would never assemble in this building again.

She had spent the season trying not to think about that. The team had gone 14 and 8, better than anyone predicted, and Natalie had started the last eleven games at point guard after Dana blew out her knee in January. Her own problems had been ordinary and pressing: her crossover was slow, her left hand weak, her father asking at dinner whether all this practice was worth the scholarship odds. She had answered him with numbers, because numbers were the only remuneration anyone recognized in this house. Fourteen and eight, she'd said. We're good.

"Hey, freshman," Dana called down, though Natalie was a junior. "Bring the sodas up. We're having a funeral."

Natalie climbed the bleachers with two cans held against her ribs. Dana had her knee braced and propped on the row below, and beside her Priya sat cross-legged with a battered spiral notebook open on her thigh. Priya was the team's only senior who cared about school more than basketball, and she was the one who had taped the practice schedule inside her AP Psych binder all season, as though the two calendars could reinforce each other.

"Read it again," Dana said.

Priya turned the notebook so Natalie could see. There were stages diagrammed in Priya's narrow handwriting, arrows connecting boxes labeled forming, storming, norming, performing. Then a fifth box, added later in different ink. "So in 1977," Priya said, "Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage." She tapped the last box. "Adjourning. That's the word."

"For what?" Natalie asked, though the hollow feeling in her chest had already guessed.

"For when a group's work ends and members separate." Priya closed the notebook. "I found it in October, and I've been waiting all season for it to be relevant. Which is a terrible way to say I knew this night would come."

Dana popped her soda and held it up. "To adjourning." The five seniors drank to it, and Priya laughed in a way that sounded like it could turn into crying, and somewhere across the gym a sophomore was shooting free throws alone, the ball's echo arriving a half second after each release.

From Priya's seat on the third row, the gym looked different than it had all season. She could see the whole court framed between Dana's braced knee and Natalie's shoulder, could see the shooting sophomore's arc repeat and repeat, and she noticed that Natalie had not drunk. Natalie was turning her can slowly in her hands, studying the label as though it might portend something about next year.

"You're quiet," Priya said to her.

"I keep thinking it doesn't have to be the fifth stage," Natalie said. "For us. Dana's coming back, right? And I'm back, and half the team's back. It's only adjourning for you two."

"Three," said Beckett, the other senior, from the end of the row. "Me too."

"Fine, three." Natalie set the can down on the bleacher, unopened. "But here's what I actually think. The thing that ends isn't the team. It's this team, this exact set of people, and that was ending from the first day of tryouts whether anybody named it or not. So maybe the model is right and I just don't like it. Or maybe a team isn't a group with a defined end, it's more like a relay, and the group is whoever's holding the baton right now." She stopped, hearing herself pile abstraction on abstraction. "I don't know which one I believe. Ask me in November."

Priya considered her for a moment, then reached over and took Natalie's unopened soda, cracked it, and drank half of it. "That's your remuneration for the philosophy," she said, handing the can back. "You'll get paid in September when the new kids look at you like you know something."

Dana pulled herself up on her crutches and stood facing the court. The light through the high windows had gone amber, and the dust in it hung like something diaphanous between the rafters and the floor, the same dust they had run through all winter. "One last thing," Dana said. "Everyone on the court. Yes, you too, Priya. Bring the ball."

They played, in the loosest sense: seniors and juniors and the startled sophomore, no score, Dana stationed at the free-throw line calling out plays she had no intention of running. Priya stood at the top of the arc with the ball and did nothing with it for a long moment, just watched all of them scattered across the floor in positions they had occupied for months. Then she bounced it once, hard, and let the sound fill the gym.

"Adjourning," she said, and passed to Natalie, who was already moving.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
story:
Jayden set his phone face down next to his plate before his mother could say anything about it. The poll results were still open in his head anyway: fifty-two percent of students wanted the college to keep the late-night shuttle, forty-eight percent wanted it cut and the money moved to mental health services. He had fifteen hundred respondents, or rather one thousand and forty, and at eleven that night the paper's website would go live with whatever headline he chose.

"Your grandmother called twice," his mother said, spooning rice onto his brother's plate. "Twice."

His brother, Ellis, who was twelve and choleric about nearly everything lately, stabbed at a chicken nugget. "Because Dad told her I quit soccer."

"You did quit soccer."

"I paused soccer."

Jayden pushed a pea to the edge of his plate. His father asked how the paper was going, the way he asked about most things, which was kindly and without any intention of following the answer past the first sentence. But Jayden answered anyway, because it was the one thing he wanted to say out loud before eleven o'clock. He told them about the survey the student government had run, that he'd gotten the raw numbers that afternoon, that his co-editor, Priya, wanted to run the headline as "Majority of Students Support Keeping Shuttle."

"Sounds right," his father said. "Fifty-two is more than fifty."

"It's four points," Jayden said.

Ellis said that four points was nothing, that his soccer team had lost by four points and it had counted as a loss. Their mother said that was football and this was not. Jayden let it go and kept going himself, slowly, because the shape of the thing was still forming while he talked. He'd spent the bus ride home with the numbers, and then an hour at the library's statistics guide before he understood what he was even looking for. One thousand and forty students had answered. It wasn't every student. It was a sample, drawn at random, and there was a rule about samples that size, a figure he'd found and written on his wrist to remember.

"Margin of error," he said. "With a simple random sample of about a thousand people, it's roughly plus or minus three percentage points."

His father's fork paused. "Three points each way."

"Each way. So fifty-two could really be forty-nine." He moved his peas again, two of them this time. "Or it could be fifty-five. And forty-eight could be fifty-one. They overlap. You can't actually tell who's ahead."

The table was quiet long enough for his mother to say, "So the poll says nothing?"

"No. It says something." This was the part he hadn't worked out until the walk home, and saying it now, in front of the chicken and the rice, made it firmer. "It says the campus is close to split. It rules out a landslide. It just doesn't rule out either side being ahead. Priya wants to say the majority supports the shuttle, and technically more of our respondents did. But if the real number for all students could be under fifty, we'd be printing a majority that might not exist."

Priya had been inured to student government's habits by two years on the beat; she assumed every release was spun until proven otherwise, and she'd been right often enough that her instinct was worth something. Jayden usually deferred to it. But instinct and a number weren't the same kind of thing, and tonight the number was his.

"Then don't say majority," his mother said. "Say students are divided."

"That's weaker," Jayden said. "Nobody clicks on 'Students Are Divided.' And the student government wants the shuttle kept, so if we run the weak headline, they'll say we buried them."

Ellis looked up. "So the truth is boring and the lie gets clicks."

"It's not a lie. It's just not proven."

His father asked whether Priya had seen the margin of error thing, and Jayden said he'd texted her a picture of the page an hour ago and she'd replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else, which meant she was either convinced or annoyed, and with Priya those looked identical from a distance. He had also texted his journalism professor, who had not replied, because the professor never replied after eight.

Ellis announced that nothing mattered anyway, that he'd learned the word existentialism in school that day and that according to the French the shuttle question was pointless because everything was. Their mother said the French could clear the table. Ellis cleared the table.

Jayden helped dry the dishes while his mother washed, and he told her the smaller version of the problem, the one he could hold in one hand: he could write that the poll found fifty-two percent in favor, and print the sample size and the margin in the sixth paragraph where nobody read, and the student government would be happy and the paper would look decisive. Or he could put the margin in the first sentence, where it made the whole poll smaller, and take the heat. He'd spent a year inuring himself to the idea that the editor's job was judgment, not arithmetic, but tonight the judgment was the arithmetic.

"Which one lets you sleep," his mother said, handing him the pot.

He thought about it honestly, which meant admitting he didn't know whether a bigger headline would matter, whether the administration would even read past the first line, whether a future editor would have to retract something he'd implied. All of that stayed uncertain. What he had was one thousand and forty random students, three points in either direction, and a decision at eleven.

In his room he opened the draft and deleted "Majority." He typed: "Students Split on Shuttle, Poll Shows, With Results Within Margin of Error." Then he texted Priya: running this unless you object by 10:30. He set the phone on the desk, screen up, and watched the three dots appear.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
story:
Ryan's grandfather kept his old law books in the sunroom, shelf after shelf of them, and that was where Ryan went first when the assignment landed in his inbox: argue both sides of a free speech case before a mock Supreme Court, alone, in front of his whole constitutional law elective. The rules said each side got eight minutes. Eight minutes to convince his classmates, and then eight minutes to convince them of the opposite.

The case his teacher had built was about a student, not much older than Ryan, who had posted a video telling people to "shut the school down, whatever it takes." Nobody had gotten hurt, but a fight had broken out in the parking lot, and the school had expelled him. Ryan's job was not to decide whether the expulsion was fair. His job was to make the best argument for the student, then turn around and make the best argument for the school, as though he believed each one down to his shoes.

He tried drafting in the kitchen and got nowhere. His grandfather drifted through for coffee, saw the sprawl of printouts, and said only, "Sunroom's quieter." That was the whole invitation. Ryan carried his papers to the long table under the window where the light was best, and for two days he let the arguments ruminate, circling each other in his head while he half-watched his grandfather putter in the garden below, a small, deliberate figure in a straw hat.

The student's side came easily. Words are not acts, Ryan wrote. A video is not a bomb. If we punish every angry thing anyone posts, we punish the impecunious kid with a phone the same as a senator with a network, and we chill the speech of everyone who might have something true and unwelcome to say. He liked that paragraph. It sounded like the editorials he admired.

The school's side was worse. Every argument he drafted felt like a police siren. He was rummaging through the shelf behind him, more out of frustration than scholarship, when he found a fat green casebook with a cracked spine, and inside it, a page his grandfather had underlined in pencil decades ago. The margin note just said, "This is the one that got away from all of us." The case was Schenck v. United States. Ryan read it twice, then a third time, and the pieces began to shift against each other like tiles in a puzzle he hadn't known he was holding.

The case had introduced a test. His grandfather's pencil led him down the margin: clear and present danger. Under it, speech could be punished if it created a clear and present danger of a harm that Congress could prevent. That was the bridge. The government side didn't have to claim that words were fists. It only had to show danger, clear and present, aimed at a harm the law was allowed to stop. Ryan sat back. His two drafts weren't opposites after all. They were two hands gripping the same scale, and the test was where the scale balanced, or failed to.

He tried it out loud that evening, standing at the sunroom table as if it were the bench. "For the school, the question isn't whether the video was offensive. It's whether it created a clear and present danger of a harm Congress could prevent." His grandfather appeared in the doorway with two mugs, set one down, and said, "Careful, though." Ryan waited. "When you argue it for the student, you're going to say that test is a hundred years old and that the Court tightened its own leash later. You'll have to hold both ideas in one head. Most people never manage it. They pick a side at seventeen and defend it at seventy." He tapped the casebook. "Underlined that before your father was born."

Ryan had planned to do exactly that, wave the test away as ancient history when it hurt his side. He sat with his coffee going cold and made himself write the harder thing instead: that the test survived in some form because every society has to answer the same question underneath it, and that utilitarianism, the trade of one speaker's freedom for many students' safety, could justify almost anything if you let it, and could justify nothing if you refused it entirely. Where the line actually fell, on a video like that one, in a parking lot like that one, he could not say. He wrote that he could not say, and left it on the page.

On the morning of the mock court, his classmates filed in with their note cards, and Ryan stood up with nothing but two pages and his grandfather's cracked green book. He argued for the student first, then took a breath, squared his shoulders, and began, "For the school, I'd ask the court to apply the clear and present danger test, and I'd ask you to notice that I used to be afraid of it."
