activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
story:
The check from the hardware store was in Tyler's back pocket all the way to his grandfather's house, folded twice, and he kept touching it through the denim like checking for a loose tooth. Two hundred and fourteen dollars for forty hours of hauling lumber and sweeping sawdust. In the kitchen his grandfather sat at the table with the bank statements spread out in front of him, a pencil behind his ear, doing whatever he did every Saturday morning while the coffee went cold.

"You look like a man with money," his grandfather said without looking up.

"First paycheck." Tyler set it on the table between the statements. "I'm trying to figure out what to do with it. Marcus says blow it on the trip to the lake. My mom says save it for books."

His grandfather tapped the pencil against the statements. "Sit down and look at this with me first." The papers were a mess of small numbers, interest posted in little columns, and at the top a figure that Tyler assumed was a typo until he traced it back through the years. There was an account his grandfather had opened when he was young, younger than Tyler, and it had been sitting there growing the whole time, mostly ignored, like a tree nobody watered that turned out to be a maple.

Tyler pulled out his phone and opened the calculator. He started with a thousand dollars, because it was a number he could imagine saving by the end of the summer if he was careful. Seven percent, compounded yearly, was what his grandfather's account earned. He multiplied it out year by year at first, then found the exponent function and jumped straight to forty, which would put him at fifty-eight, his grandfather's age almost exactly. The phone said 14,974. He did it again to be sure. Almost fifteen thousand dollars from one thousand.

"Grandpa." He turned the phone around. "A thousand at seven percent, forty years. Look."

His grandfather put on his glasses and held the phone at arm's length. "That's about right," he said. "That's what mine did."

"So the money I put in now is worth ten times more than money I put in later. Like, at forty." Tyler was talking faster than he meant to. "Marcus says you can't prognosticate forty years out, anything could happen, I could be dead, the bank could fold, whatever. But it's not really a prediction, is it? It's just arithmetic."

"It's arithmetic until you need the money for something at thirty," his grandfather said. "Then it's a decision you already made." He said it flatly, not unkindly, and Tyler remembered that his grandfather had wanted to buy the lot next door when he was forty and hadn't had the cash, because it was all in this account, because he'd made a decision at nineteen that he was still living inside.

His grandmother came in from the garden with tomatoes in her shirt hem and set them in the sink. She had been trying for months to get his grandfather to drive down to Dayton for his brother's seventieth birthday, and there had been nothing Tyler could call a fight, just a silence with a shape to it, and she wanted the rapprochement more than either of the brothers would admit to wanting it. "Tyler, tell your grandfather he's being stubborn," she said. "You're young, he'll listen to you."

"I'm being careful," his grandfather said. "There's a difference."

"There's a pithy remark in there somewhere, I'm sure," she said, and went back to the tomatoes.

Tyler sat with the two things side by side, the phone screen and the folded check. His grandfather had locked money away at eighteen and it had grown into something he couldn't touch without undoing his own younger self's plan. That could be wisdom or that could be a cage, and the arithmetic couldn't tell him which, because the arithmetic only said what happened to the money, not what happened to the man who couldn't spend it. Maybe Marcus was right that you couldn't see forty years ahead. But maybe you didn't have to see it, only decide whether you wanted to be the kind of person who had already acted on it. He couldn't get those two thoughts to settle into one clean position, and he tried saying so.

"I think I'll put in a hundred now and keep a hundred for the lake," he said finally. "Both. And I don't know if that's smart or if it's just me not choosing."

His grandfather laughed, a short sound, and pulled a deposit slip from the drawer where the stamps were. He slid it across the table and picked up the pencil. "Your uncle Wes did the same split at your age. You can ask him yourself at the party." He looked over at the sink. "We're going to Dayton, Ruth. Book the room."

His grandmother turned around with a tomato still in her hand, and Tyler bent his head over the deposit slip and began, slowly, to fill it out.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
story:
Sophie had the financial aid letter open in two windows at once, the PDF on the left and a loan calculator on the right, because her father always said never trust a single source, and because the numbers were not behaving the way she had assumed they would. The letter offered her a Direct Subsidized loan of three thousand five hundred dollars and a Direct Unsubsidized loan of two thousand more, and until that afternoon she had treated the two words as bureaucratic decoration, interchangeable labels sedimentary with the rest of the paperwork, layers of official language that had settled into one undifferentiated mass. She was seventeen and had until May first to decide.

Her mother was in the kitchen frying onions, a sound Sophie could hear through Sophie's open door, the hiss and catch of oil in the pan. Her mother wanted her to go to the state school forty minutes away, wanted it so openly that she had begun saying "when you're home on weekends" instead of "if," and Sophie had not corrected her in weeks because the correction felt like an argument she wasn't ready to win twice in the same month. The dorm deposit for the faraway school was due the same day as the loan decision, and both of them knew it.

Sophie typed the subsidized amount into the calculator, then read the letter again, slowly, the way her English teacher had taught her to read a poem, sentence by sentence. For the subsidized loan, the government pays the interest while the student is in school. She sat back. She read the next line, which said, in plainer and colder language, that for the unsubsidized loan, interest builds during that same time, while she was sitting in lectures and pulling all-nighters and not paying anyone anything. She had not known that. She had half-known it, the way you half-know that meat has to reach a certain temperature, but now it was on the screen in front of her with a dollar sign attached.

She called Dev, who had done all this the year before and spent most of freshman fall lambasting his own past self in the group chat for what he called his "blissful illiteracy." He answered on the second ring, wind and footsteps behind him.

"Did you know the subsidized one doesn't grow while you're in school?" she asked. "The government pays the interest until you graduate. The unsubsidized one just sits there building the whole time."

"Yeah," Dev said. "Found out in October. Take the subsidized first, obviously. It's a reprieve, not a gift, but still. What are you actually deciding, though? Which school?"

Both of them, she thought. The loan was really a school question wearing a disguise. She turned in her chair and looked at the corkboard above the desk, where the two acceptance letters hung, the state school's crested paper half covering the other one, which she had pinned slightly crooked on purpose, so it would look casual, so nobody, including her, would think she cared too much.

Her mother appeared in the doorway with a wooden spoon, onion smell preceding her. "Dev says take the subsidized," Sophie told her, because telling her anything about the loans meant telling her something about the schools, and because her mother had a right to the numbers even if she would use them as ammunition.

"What's the difference?" her mother asked. Sophie said it again, the government pays the interest on one while you're in school, and on the other one the interest builds during those years, and her mother stood very still with the spoon dripping.

"So the cheap one is smaller," her mother said at last.

"Three and a half thousand versus two thousand more, but the two thousand costs more by the time I graduate, because it grows the whole way through."

Her mother nodded slowly, the way she nodded at medical bills, and said, "The state school would cost less than either," and went back to the kitchen, and the onions had gone quiet, which meant she was standing at the stove not cooking.

Sophie opened a savings account page in a third window, because the calculator had a second tab she'd been ignoring, one that ran the numbers the other direction. If she put her whole paycheck from the garden center into savings starting in June, the interest would grow her money over the same four years that the other interest would be growing the debt, two curves moving in opposite directions, and she sat for a while watching the little graph breathe. She thought about telling her mother that interest was not the enemy, that it was just a direction, and that the whole decision was choosing which direction to face. She did not say it. Her mother was entitled to her arithmetic too.

Sophie printed the aid letter, took down the crooked acceptance, and pinned the letter over it, straight, both corners. Then she went to the kitchen and said, "Smells good," and reached over her mother's shoulder to steal a piece of onion off the spoon.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
story:
Andrew had eleven paintings and room for ten. He laid them across the backyard grass in the long light of late afternoon, weighing them down at the corners with stones from the flowerbed so the wind off the hills couldn't shuffle his sequence. The application wanted a single theme, ten works, and a statement of two hundred words explaining what held them together. His theme was the water tower at the end of Miller Road, the rusted green one everyone drove past without looking, and he had painted it in rain, in August glare, behind the pharmacy sign, reflected in a puddle shaped like a lung. Eleven times.

His sister Dana came out with two glasses of iced tea and stood at the edge of the arrangement with her shoes on the concrete, unwilling to step into it. "You look like you're playing war," she said.

"I'm deciding who survives." He said it lightly, but the choosing had gone on for three days, and he had started to talk to the paintings the way their father talked to the car. The weakest one, he knew, was the fog study, because fog let him avoid the tower's ugly riveted band, and he'd solved that by hiding the hardest part. But the strongest one might be the fog study too, for exactly the same reason. He couldn't tell which instinct to trust, the craftsman's or the coward's, or whether they were the same instinct wearing different hats.

Dana crouched, still on the concrete, and drank her tea. "What do you do with the extra?"

"Delete it. Burn it. There's a rule." He picked up the fog study and held it against the light, as if honesty might show through from the back. "Ten means ten. It's a plebiscite, kind of. They ask ten people, sorry, ten paintings, to vote on who I am."

"That's not what plebiscite means," Dana said, and he knew that, actually; the number was the thing being voted on, not the paintings, and he'd used the word wrong on purpose to make the problem sound civic and therefore solvable. She let it go, which was her way of not letting it go.

He set the painting down and did what he always did when a rule felt like a wall: he looked for the wall's history. His phone still worked out here if he stood near the fence. He typed the name of the only artist his grandmother had ever loved, the Japanese one, the wave. The first result was the series, Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, and beneath the title, almost as an aside, the detail he needed: the series actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well. He read it twice. Thirty-six in the name, forty-six on the table, the title never corrected, the extra ten simply absorbed. Nobody had historicized it as a scandal. It had become part of the work.

"Listen," he said, and read the fact aloud to Dana, every number of it, the thirty-six and the forty-six and the ten added after the first sold well. She squinted at him over her glass.

"So the rule was the title, and the work outgrew the title, and nobody died."

"Nobody died." He turned his phone off and stood there among his eleven towers while a jay complained from the mulberry. He understood that one thing had changed and one thing hadn't. The Hokusai fact gave him permission to think of ten as a beginning rather than a verdict, a floor instead of a ceiling; the application deadline, however, did not care what Hokusai did, and would still reject forty-six if it asked for thirty-six. He could hold both thoughts at once, which felt less like a solution than like learning to carry two full glasses without spilling either. He still didn't know if the fog study was courage or avoidance. That part might stay uncertain, and he was tired of pretending the uncertainty was temporary.

He went inside for the good pencil and came back with his grandmother's loquacious parakeet on his shoulder, the bird having escaped the kitchen again through the gap above the doorframe. He knelt in the grass, took the statement draft from under a stone, and crossed out his first sentence, the one that claimed the tower "revealed the hidden order of the ordinary." In its place he wrote: "I painted the water tower eleven times because ten was not enough and eleven was too many, and this portfolio is the argument for the ten that were enough." Then he moved the fog study out of the row and set it face down on the patio, not deleted, not chosen, just waiting.

Dana raised her glass to it. "For the eleventh view," she said, and Andrew laughed and taped the new sentence into the statement, the parakeet gripping his collar and leaning toward the paper as though it meant to read.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Alyssa's garage smelled of motor oil and old carpet, and in the corner between the lawnmower and a shelf of paint cans, her uncle's violin had hung for three years in a case nobody opened. She had claimed it in March, after the community center posted a notice about a beginner strings group, and every evening since she dragged a folding chair into the rectangle of light under the single bulb and practiced until her left fingertips went numb.

The problem was the tuning. Her teacher at the center, a college sophomore who ran the rehearsals like a benevolent dictator, had told them all to download the same tuner app and to come to Thursday's rehearsal already in tune. Alyssa had assumed tuning meant making the strings sound pleasant together. Instead the app wanted something exact, a number, and she sat in the garage turning the fine tuners a hair at a time while the needle on her cracked phone screen swung between two green bars like a needle deciding a life sentence.

"You're sharp again," her brother Marcus said from the workbench, where he was supposed to be cleaning a bike chain and was instead supervising. "Flat. Whatever the sad one is."

"Flat," she said, because she had learned that much. The app read the pitch of her open A string in hertz, and the target was 440. Not 438, not 442, because the whole world, apparently, had agreed. Her phone showed the standard as a line of small text she'd read so often she could recite it: the note was A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization. She'd looked up the organization out of stubbornness and found the standard went by a name, ISO 16, an ordinary fact filed like a birth certificate.

Marcus picked up the tuner phone and held it next to the violin's A string, plucking it with a greasy thumb. "Four hundred forty," he read. "You did it."

She hadn't, exactly. The needle hovered at 440 and then drifted, and she turned the peg a millimeter and it dropped to 436, and she thought, not for the first time, that her grandmother's old aphorism about close enough only counting in horseshoes had never felt less comforting. Her grandmother had said it about Alyssa quitting piano at nine, and Alyssa had resented it for years without being able to say why. Now she suspected the resentment was that the aphorism was true and she had been the horseshoe.

At the Thursday rehearsal, the room smelled like floor wax and someone's microwaved soup. Twenty-two beginners sat in a semicircle, and before anything else the college sophomore walked the rows with a small speaker, playing one note into the room. "We all tune to this," she said. "A four forty. Same as your apps. Otherwise we'd sound like an argument." Alyssa matched her A to it and for the first time heard her own string align with forty others, a sound like a door sliding open.

Rafi, the cellist beside her, had tuned to his ear instead of the app, and during the first piece the sophomore stopped the group twice because of a sourness no one could locate. The third time she stood behind the cellos with the speaker, patient, and Rafi adjusted. Afterward he told Alyssa his grandfather in Lahore had tuned by ear his whole life, no standard at all, and had still been the best musician anyone knew. "So which is it," Rafi asked, not really asking, "four forty or the ear?"

She turned the question over on the drive home, Marcus driving, the violin flat on the back seat like a passenger. Rafi's grandfather had made music without the number; the number had made the room full of strangers into one instrument. Both were true at once, and she could not flatten them into a single principle, and she found she preferred it that way, the way she preferred a chord with a little tension in it. When they pulled into the driveway the garage door was already up, the bulb burning, her grandmother standing inside holding the piano tuner's card that had arrived in the mail that afternoon, addressed to the house. "Found this in the box with your uncle's things," her grandmother said. "They can come Tuesday."

"For what?" Alyssa asked.

"Your uncle's piano," her grandmother said, patting the dust cover over the shapes underneath it, the shapes Alyssa had assumed were a workbench all along. "It's been flat for years."

The pamphlet on the desk between them had a lighthouse on it, which Jordan took as a bad sign, since he was fairly sure there were no lighthouses within four hours of his hometown. "This is the maritime engineering program," Ms. Andaya said, tapping it. "Full ride. Your father's plant recruits straight out of it." Behind her, a motivational poster of a mountain range rippled slightly whenever the radiator kicked on, the plastic laminate seeming to undulate, as though even the stock photograph could not commit to staying still.

"I also have the audition," Jordan said. "Chicago. February ninth." He did not say conservatory, because the word made his father's jaw do a thing.

Ms. Andaya turned to her keyboard. He watched her type his name and then, in a separate field, a number he could not read upside down, though he tried. The radiator clicked off and the mountain range froze. "You can't be in Chicago and at the scholarship weekend at the same time," she said. "I checked. Same dates. I'm sorry."

He had known that already, of course, but hearing it spoken in a room that smelled of instant coffee and dying spider plants made it heavier, the way things get heavier when someone with a filing cabinet says them.

At the coffee shop that evening, Dev had his economics syllabus spread across the table, holding it down with a mug with a chip in the rim. Jordan read upside down, which was a skill he'd developed in biology, and one line snagged him. "What is 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which is Not Seen'?" Dev looked at the page as if he'd never seen it before, which was possible, since Dev's relationship with syllabi was famously noncommittal. "Bastiat. Some French economist, 1850. My professor says he'll base half the midterm on it." Jordan waited. "The idea is, like, good economics has to count the effects nobody sees. The stuff that doesn't happen because something else did."

Jordan turned his cup a quarter turn on its saucer, then another quarter. "Say a town breaks a window." He had this half-formed from Dev's shrugging summary, and he was trying to build the rest. "Everyone says, look, work for the glazier, money moving around. Good news. But nobody sees the shoes the shopkeeper was going to buy instead. The shoes never existed. Nobody can point at them."

"Sure," Dev said, already back to highlighting. "Opportunity cost, basically."

Jordan did not say anything for a while, long enough that Dev looked up. In the window behind him, the lights of the parking lot had come on, and beyond them, faintly, the hill with the water tower. Somewhere past that hill was Chicago, and somewhere past that, presumably, a life in which he had not spent four years learning sonatas in a practice room with a chair that wobbled. Neither of those lives could be pointed at either. He had been walking around thinking he had two futures in his pocket, and it occurred to him now, with a small internal lurch that was almost funny, that he had at most one, and that picking it was the same act as killing the other. There was a version of the feeling that felt tragic and a version that felt like simple arithmetic, and he could not decide which was bathos and which was honesty.

At home his father asked how the appointment went. Jordan said the scholarship weekend and the audition were the same dates. His father nodded slowly, the way he nodded when a machine on the line was doing something expensive. "Well," his father said. "You always knew it might come to that." There it was: nobody in the family had ever once said the word conservatory out loud, as though not naming it kept it cheap, kept it a hobby, kept it out of the ledger where real things were counted. Jordan thought that this kind of not-naming was practically endemic to their house, and that he had caught it too, and that he was probably doing it right now.

The next morning he went back to Ms. Andaya before first period, without an appointment, and stood in her doorway with his hands in his jacket pockets. She raised her eyebrows over a yogurt cup. "I have a question," he said. "When people talk about the scholarship, they keep saying eighty thousand dollars. What I'd get. That's the seen thing, right?" She set down the spoon. "And the thing I'd give up, nobody can put a number on it, so they talk like it's nothing. Like it doesn't exist because you can't invoice it."

Ms. Andaya regarded him for a moment, then pulled the maritime pamphlet toward her and slid it into the drawer, unopened. "That's a more interesting question than most people bring me," she said. "I don't have the answer to it. I want to be clear that I don't."

"I know." He rocked once on his heels. "I mostly wanted to say it out loud in a room with a filing cabinet."

She laughed, which she almost never did, and handed him the audition form instead of taking it from him, and said, "Then get your father to sign this one. And use my printer, it's faster than the library's."

story:
The plastic apron was too big for Rebecca, and she kept wiping her hands on it as though it were a napkin. St. Brigid's had put her on the serving line at six-thirty sharp, next to a man named Cyrus who ladled soup with the calm of someone who had done it a thousand times. Her volunteer hours were due by Friday, forty of them, and she had left this last shift until the end because, she admitted to herself on the walk over, she had been afraid of it. She'd imagined gratitude, and gratitude made her flinch. What she found instead was a line of people who mostly didn't look at her, who held out trays and said thank you and moved on, and this turned out to be easier and harder than she had feared.

The trouble started with the bread. A woman with a bruise on her cheekbone asked whether there was anything gluten-free, and there wasn't, and the woman took the bread anyway, and Rebecca stood there holding the tongs feeling that she had failed at something without being able to name it. Later a boy, maybe her own age, asked for seconds before the line had finished its first pass. She looked at Cyrus, and Cyrus shook his head once, almost invisible, and she had to say no. "We hold some back," Cyrus said quietly, when the boy had gone to a table. "If we run out before the line ends, that's worse." She understood the arithmetic of it, and still the boy's face stayed with her.

At eight, a white van pulled up to the dock, and out of it came a short, fast-moving woman named Dot, carrying crates of bread still smelling of the oven. Rebecca was sent to help her stack them. "From my restaurant," Dot said. "We bake too much on purpose, honestly, because the lunch crowd is unpredictable, and my business partner calls the leftovers my nemesis. Every night, thirty loaves with nowhere to go." She laughed at that, hefting a crate onto the shelf.

"You can just give it away?" Rebecca asked. She was thinking of a story her father told, some man sued over a donated sandwich, though the details had gone soft in her memory.

"That's what people used to be afraid of," Dot said. "You give somebody food, they say it made them sick, they sue you, your restaurant dies. Most places wouldn't risk it. Then Congress fixed it." She slid the last crate home. "It's called the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act, 1996. It gives donors limited protection from liability. So now I don't lie awake over bread."

Rebecca turned the words over while she carried the empty crates back out. Limited protection. She liked that it wasn't absolute; it sounded like a law that had been argued over, some compromise between the people afraid of being sued and the people afraid of the waste. Her mother, who was a lawyer, would say something about how every protection has a boundary drawn somewhere, and the whole fight is about where. Rebecca didn't know where this one was drawn, and Dot hadn't said, and she found she preferred not knowing to pretending the law had solved everything.

The boy from earlier was still at his table, reading a paperback with a cracked spine, his bread untouched beside an empty soup bowl. She checked with Cyrus first this time, and he nodded, and she carried a bowl over. "We held some back," she said, setting it down. He looked up at her, then at the bowl, and said, "I was going to ask again, but I figured you'd get in trouble." She hadn't thought about trouble, actually. She had thought about running out.

While she wiped down the serving line, she tried to say to Cyrus what she was sorting out, that the rules were necessary and the rules were insufficient, and that both things could be true at once, but it came out clumsy and she stopped halfway. "It's germane, though," she said, "isn't it, the part about holding back. That it only works if someone also breaks the rule a little." Cyrus considered this, wringing out his rag.

"I'd say it works because someone thought about it ahead of time," he said. "The holding back is in the rules now. You just didn't know them yet."

Rebecca untied the apron and folded it, and it occurred to her that she still had an hour before her ride came. She went back out to the dock, where Dot was relocking the van. "Could I come by the restaurant sometime," Rebecca asked, "to see how much bread there is? Like, actually count it?" Dot squinted at her, and then grinned. "Come Tuesday," she said. "That's the day my nemesis absconds with the most."

story:
Gavin had put it off until October of grade eleven, and now the form sat on the kitchen table like a summons: forty hours of community involvement, printed in the school's gray ink, required before the Ontario Secondary School Diploma would be his. His mother had slid it under his door that morning without comment. By noon he was standing in the loading bay of the Weston Food Bank in a borrowed apron, watching a woman named Mara point at a metal cart.

"Sort by date. Oldest in front. Anything dented goes on the shelf behind you."

He took the cart and wheeled it toward the pallet, but a girl with a ponytail and a lanyard pulled it out of his hands and began stacking cans at double speed.

"I need this one," she said.

"There are four others."

"Mine's faster."

He let her have it, then went and took one of the others, and for a while they worked the same pallet from opposite ends, competing without saying so. Her lanyard read Volunteer Since September, and underneath it, in ballpoint, she had written a tally of numbers that climbed toward some total he couldn't see.

"Priya," she said finally, not looking up. "Grade twelve."

"Gavin. Eleven."

"Lucky." She set a can of peas in the front row, perfectly flush. "Forty hours of community involvement to graduate, and my sheet's got twelve left on it, and the diploma deadline doesn't care about my midterm schedule." She said it flat, the way you report weather. "So I'm here every Saturday until it's done."

He wanted to say something decent, and what came out was, "I'm here so I never have to be in your position." She laughed once, without warmth, and passed him a case of soup.

Two hours in, he opened a donation box that someone had left in the vestibule overnight, and a folded page slid out from between bags of pasta. He nearly put it in recycling before he saw the handwriting. Dear whoever sorts this, it began. Times are bad at our house but better than last year, so here is what I would have needed then. Use it well. There was no signature, only a smear where a label had been. He read it twice, then folded it small and put it in his back pocket, and did not tell Priya.

He knew about needing things. In grade six, the year his father's warehouse job ended, a box had appeared on their porch on three separate Thursday nights, never the same Thursdays, and his mother would carry it in fast, like something that might be taken back. He had been allowed to pick the cereal. He remembered choosing carefully, seriously, the way you choose when it's the only choice you'll get that week. They never spoke about it, and when the boxes stopped, they didn't speak about that either.

"Your essay again?" Priya asked at the break table, nodding at his phone. He had been reading a philosophy summary for Monday's class, and he angled the screen away.

"It's about whether things have a purpose built into them. Teleology. The idea that what something is for is part of what it is."

"So a can of soup is for feeding people."

"The can's for storing soup. The food bank's for feeding people. Maybe." He turned his phone face down. "Or maybe it's just for me to get a diploma, and the feeding part is a side effect."

"That's grim." She bit into her sandwich. "Also it's backwards. The feeding's the point. The diploma's the side effect you get for showing up." She said it like it was obvious, and he couldn't decide whether she was right or whether she just needed to be.

After the break, Mara put them on the obsolete freezer, a walk-in whose compressor had failed in August and which now held nothing but shelving and an obsolescent invoice printer nobody had removed. Priya commandeered the rolling ladder and stripped the labels while Gavin hauled the printer to the dock. When he came back, she was standing very still at the top of the ladder.

"Eleven hours," she said. "She's counting today as three. One left after this."

"Then you're done."

"Then I'm done."

At closing, Mara sat at the front desk with the sign-in binder and asked Priya first. Priya held out her sheet, and Mara wrote the date and the hours and the total, forty of forty, and stamped it, and Priya stared at the stamp the way you stare at a finish line you're not sure you wanted to reach. Then it was Gavin's turn, and Mara held out her pen.

"You'll want me to log today," she said. "Three hours toward your forty."

He looked at his own sheet, nearly empty, and at Priya's, finished, and at the folded note in his mind's pocket. He pulled his sheet back before she could write on it.

"Can you hold off until the end of the month?" he said. "I'll be back Saturdays anyway. Sign it all at once."

Priya paused at the door with her stamped sheet in her fist.

"You're going to volunteer," she said slowly, "and not count the hours."

"Next Saturday," Gavin said, taking the apron from the hook.

story:
Austin had the paycheque open in one window and a calculator open in the other, and he kept catching himself leaning closer to the screen as if the numbers might rearrange themselves if he got near enough. Twelve hours of stocking shelves at the garden centre, that was the top line. Then the lines below it, each one taking a small bite: federal income tax, state income tax, something called FICA. He'd expected the gross amount and the net amount to be different, but he hadn't expected the difference to feel like this, like watching someone eat off his plate.

He screenshotted it and sent it to his mother, who was still at work, then thought better of it and typed instead, "Is this right?" She replied with a thumbs up and the words "welcome to adulthood," which he found simultaneously funny and scathing, though he couldn't have said which part was which.

The laptop was the point of all this. His old one had died in March with a sound like a spoon in a garbage disposal, and since then he'd been doing everything on his phone, including the college application he was supposed to be finishing before September. He had $640 saved. The machine he wanted, the one that would last all four years if he was careful, was $899 in the big-box store fifteen minutes from his house, and with sales tax it came to $956 and change. He'd done that math three times tonight, hovering over the store's page, watching the total climb at checkout like water rising in a locked room.

That was when Dex called. Dex wanted to talk about orientation, about his roommate assignment, about a girl named Priya, but Austin was only half listening until Dex said, "Wait, where are you at with the laptop?"

"Sixteen dollars short of hopeless," Austin said. "Why?"

"Because my cousin lives in Delaware," Dex said. "Five states have no sales tax. Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, Oregon. No statewide sales tax, none. My uncle drives down there to buy furniture."

Austin pulled the phone away from his ear and stared at it, then put it back. "That can't be right."

"Look it up, then. I'm telling you, Delaware. Priya's from there, that's how it came up. She says people cross the border from like four different states just to shop."

He opened a new tab while Dex kept talking about Priya's opinion of the orientation schedule. He typed the question into the search bar the way you'd test a rumour, expecting to be corrected. Instead the fact sat there in five different sources, plain as a weather report. Delaware. No sales tax. He did the arithmetic again, this time without the tax, and the number came out under his savings by almost forty dollars.

"Hello," Dex said. "Did you die?"

"I'm here. I'm doing math." Austin sat back. Here was the thing he hadn't said to anyone, the encumbrance he'd been carrying since April: he'd turned down the overnight inventory shift in June because Marcus was having his going-away party, one night, one stupid night, and it had cost him roughly ninety dollars net. If he'd worked it, he'd have the laptop already, tax or no tax, and no need for anybody's cousin or anybody's border. He told Dex this, the whole embarrassing arithmetic of it, and Dex was quiet for a second.

"You'd still skip the party," Dex said. It wasn't a question.

"I don't know. That's what I keep landing on. I don't know." And he found he meant it in both directions at once, which was a strange place to stand. He believed in showing up for people; Marcus had driven him to the emergency room sophomore year over a wrist he'd broken in a way neither of them liked to describe. But he also wanted, with a steadiness that surprised him, to walk into college with a machine that worked. It felt like the choice was between two selves, and he was tired of pretending they were the same self.

"So drive to Delaware," Dex said. "It's like two hours. Priya says there's a micro center or whatever right over the line. You buy it, you bring it back, done."

Austin pulled up the map. Two hours and ten minutes, each way, in his mother's car, which he'd have to ask for, and which got thirty-one miles to the gallon. He did that math too, because apparently that was who he was now. Gas, roughly twenty dollars. A day of his summer. He sat there with the cursor blinking in the search bar and thought about how the tax code, the whole elaborate scaffolding he'd glimpsed on his paycheque, was built by people making exactly these calculations, deciding where money was worth going and where it wasn't. He had never thought of it as something you could route around. He had never thought of it as a landscape at all, with borders and crossings and quiet little exemptions the way some people apparently had cousins.

"There's one thing," he said. "If I buy it there and something breaks, the warranty stuff, the returns. I'd be two hours from the store."

"So mail it in."

"So mail it in," Austin repeated. His mother would be home at six. He could have the route mapped, could have his case ready, the numbers lined up like an argument he almost believed in. Almost, because underneath it he could still hear the party, the sound of Marcus's backyard that night, the fire pit and the laughing, none of which appeared on any receipt.

He typed a message to Priya, whom he'd met exactly once: "Dex says you're from Delaware. Is it actually worth the drive?" Then he sat with his hands off the keyboard, waiting, while outside a neighbour's sprinkler ticked across a lawn and the screen held both his questions open at once.

story:
Kaitlyn had spread the prospectuses across the corner table like a dealer laying out cards she didn't want to play. Six of them. Behind the counter, the espresso machine hissed and went quiet, hissed and went quiet, marking time the way the clock over the pastry case refused to. Her laptop was open to the UCAS page, the cursor blinking in the box where her choices would go. The deadline was midnight.

"You're still here," Dev said, dropping into the seat across from her with his own cup. He worked three evenings a week at the place and knew her order, her table, and her habit of staying until closing. He glanced at the paper wall. "That's six."

"That's six," she agreed. She slid one toward him, then pulled it back before he could touch it. "History at St Andrews. English at Durham. English at Manchester. History at Bristol. Liberal Arts at Nottingham. And Archaeology at Newcastle."

"Archaeology?"

"Don't start."

"Starting." He sipped his coffee. "How many can you put down?"

"Five courses. That's the limit." She turned the laptop so he could see the page, the five empty slots. "And the thing is, it doesn't matter what order you list them in. They're all just there. No ranking, no first choice, nothing. Five courses, and the universities can't tell which one you actually want." She said it flatly, like a fact she'd memorized and now resented.

"So cut one." He picked up the Newcastle prospectus anyway, flipping through pictures of trenches and potsherds. "This one, obviously."

"It's not obvious." She took it back from him. The truth was she'd been arguing with herself for a week, and the argument had stopped moving. Her father wanted Durham, had wanted Durham since she was eleven, and wanted it in the way that made disagreement feel like theft. Her mother had only said "any of them are good, love," which helped nothing, because it was tautological: good schools are good, and Kaitlyn already knew that. What she wanted to know was which of the six she would still want in March, when the offers came back or didn't.

The pressure had started as a small thing, a tightness in her chest when she opened the laptop each evening. Lately it had spread to her hands. Last night she'd caught herself unable to type her own personal statement password, fingers hovering. Her plan had been to cauterize the whole problem in one sitting, tonight, to burn the choice closed and stop feeling it. It wasn't working. Every time she reached for the delete key on one prospectus, she thought of a reason it belonged and a reason it didn't, and both reasons sounded exactly as strong.

"You know what your gran would say," Dev said.

"Don't."

"She'd say something short and annoying. Like an epigram. 'A short list is a long goodbye,' or whatever."

"See, that's the problem with epigrams. They sound true whether or not they are." She stacked the prospectuses and squared the edges against the table. Then, because squaring them was easier than choosing, she did it again.

Dev watched her do it twice. "Okay. Which one would you pick if your dad had never heard of Durham?"

She didn't answer right away. The machine hissed. Someone at the counter asked for oat milk and got told they were out. "Not English at Durham," she said finally. "But that's not how it works. He has heard of it."

"But the unis can't see the order," Dev said. "You told me. Five courses, no preference shown. So if you put down all the English ones and one History, nobody knows which is the real one." He shrugged. "Except you."

She looked at the screen, the five blank lines that would hold whatever she gave them. The Archaeology prospectus sat on top of the stack, a trench on its cover, students in hi-vis vests crouched in dirt. There was something in the picture she couldn't name: patience, maybe, the willingness to work slowly at something buried. That was the part of her nobody's plans had room for, not her father's, not even really her own.

"Six minutes to close," Dev said, standing, gathering empty cups from the next table.

She deleted English at Manchester first, then hesitated, fingers over the keys, the Newcastle booklet still in her left hand.

"Kaitlyn."

"One second." She typed something, deleted it, typed it again. Outside, a bus went past, lit up, carrying people somewhere at this hour, and she hit submit before she could change her mind about whatever it was she had decided.

story:
The email arrived at 4:17 on a Thursday, and Ashton read it three times before it settled into meaning. The district's new early-warning system had flagged him as "at risk of not completing the term," and his counselor wanted a meeting Monday morning. He sat at his desk with his hands off the keyboard, listening to his mother's television murmuring through the wall, because the thing was absurd. His grades were fine. His attendance was fine. Something in the system had looked at him, or at something near him, and decided.

He opened the student portal and found the appeal form, then discovered the form wanted a reason code. There was no code for "the machine is wrong about me." He typed a draft, deleted it, typed another. Behind him the window darkened by glacial degrees, the last of the light crawling off the bookshelf.

Dara answered on the second ring, her voice already skeptical. "You got flagged? For what?"

"They won't say. The email says factors may include attendance, grades, disciplinary records, and 'engagement data.' Engagement data. That's the surveillance part. It counts logins, clicks, how long I leave an assignment open."

"So they're watching everybody all the time and grading you on it."

"Basically." He pulled up the district's page on the system while she talked, scrolling through paragraphs of cheerful language about "proactive support." Somewhere in a footnote he found a link to the vendor's own documentation, and there, in a section on training data, a sentence about how the model had been calibrated on past students. Past students. He thought about who the past students were, where the school sat in their part of the city, what "engagement" might have looked like in a household with one shared laptop and three kids. He didn't say any of this out loud yet. He wasn't sure enough.

Marcus showed up at the coffee shop Saturday with his laptop bag over one shoulder and an opinion already loaded. "You're overthinking it. The system's new. They'll work the kinks out. It's too early to have rules about this stuff, the technology barely exists."

"It exists in my inbox," Ashton said.

"That's one email."

Dara set her cup down with more force than the cup deserved. "It's fifty thousand kids, Marcus. It's not too early. It's too late. Everybody's already in it."

They went back and forth, Marcus insisting regulation would strangle a useful tool, Dara insisting the tool was already strangling people, and Ashton sat between them feeling both arguments as true. That night he typed the argument into the search bar almost as a joke, the way you ask the internet to settle a fight it can't settle. The answer that came back stopped him. A philosopher named David Collingridge, in a book from 1980, had put a name to exactly this. His friend at the next table in the library, when Ashton showed him the page, read it and said, "The Collingridge dilemma."

"What's the dilemma part?"

"You can't predict what a technology will do when it's new, and by the time you can see what it does, it's too dug in to change. That's the trap." The friend slid the laptop back. "Nineteen eighty. Before any of this."

Ashton read the page twice, and something in him unclenched, because the trap had a shape now. It wasn't that Marcus was dumb or Dara was paranoid. They were standing at two ends of the same dilemma and calling each other wrong. But the shape also told him something harder: knowing the trap existed didn't spring it open. He couldn't see any clean way out, and he suspected no one could, not yet.

On Sunday he did the boring thing, which was the only thing he could see to do. He filled out the appeal form with no reason code attached, and instead he wrote, in the comment box, three paragraphs: what the system had said about him, what he had found in the vendor's documentation about training data, and a question about whether students and families could review the "engagement" data themselves. He made himself enunciate each sentence as he typed it, half under his breath, the way he practiced for debate, because if the words were going to stand up in front of a committee they had better be said clearly at least once. He wasn't asking them to scrap the system. He was asking for a door in it, a way for a person to walk in and check the machine's work. Small, maybe glacially slow. But Monday morning he was going to sit in that office, put the printed page on the counselor's desk, and start with the question.

The resolution said "This house would lower the voting age to sixteen," and Julia was arguing for it, which meant that Marcus Okafor was about to argue against her, which meant she would lose, probably, the way she always lost to Marcus, who had read every book in the school library with the word "logic" in the title and wore this fact like a badge.

She stood at the podium waiting for his rebuttal, and the flaw in her own case rose up to meet her. She had said that sixteen-year-olds work, pay taxes on their paychecks, drive cars, and manage course loads that would stagger a Rhodes scholar, none of which, she now saw, proved anything about voting. Marcus would point that out. Marcus would take her weakest sentence, hold it up like a dropped glove, and hammer it while the real question sat untouched behind him.

He began, as he always did, with a definition. "Democracy," he said, "presumes a capacity for long-horizon judgment that neuroscience tells us is not fully developed until the mid-twenties." There was more, about insurance premiums and rental cars and why no one let sophomores sign mortgages, and the judges wrote things down, and Julia wrote things down too, because something odd was happening. She was writing his argument, not her response to it. She had filled half a page before she noticed.

The night before, her father had refused to extend her curfew past eleven. "Because I said so," he had finished, which was, as adages go, less an adage than a surrender. Julia had wanted to scream that he was treating her like a child, and instead she heard herself say, slowly, like walking on ice: "If I understand you, you'd say that the road home is badly lit after eleven, and that the stretch past the canal has no sidewalk, and that you'd be asleep and unable to come get me if something went wrong. Is that your reason? Because it's a better reason than the one you gave." Her father had put down his fork. He had looked at her for a long moment and said, "That's what I meant." They had settled on eleven-thirty and a text at the corner of Marsh Street, and Julia had gone upstairs feeling as though she'd performed a magic trick whose mechanism she didn't understand.

Marcus sat down. It was her turn, and she had a page of his reasoning in front of her, and she made a decision that felt like stepping off a ledge. "My opponent's argument," she said, "is actually stronger than he made it. He said neuroscience. He didn't need to. Here is his case at its best." She laid it out: judgment matures late; we already restrict rights on that basis; voting requires weighing distant consequences against present impulses; therefore the franchise should track maturity, not enthusiasm. She added the part Marcus had only implied, that working and paying tax doesn't confer a right to control the money's use, any more than paying rent makes you the landlord. "That," she said, "is the steel-man. It's the practice of restating the opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than they put it, before you answer it." Marcus's eyebrows moved a quarter inch, which for Marcus was applause.

Then, and only then, she responded. If maturity is the standard, she said, the test should be maturity, not birthday, and plenty of adults would fail a long-horizon judgment test while plenty of sophomores would pass it, so either we screen everyone or we screen no one, and screening everyone is a project no one in this room, including her opponent, actually wants. She heard herself use the word "if" four times, building little conditional houses and walking through their rooms. If the brain matures at twenty-five, then why eighteen for everything else. If eighteen is arbitrary, then the argument isn't about sixteen at all. Marcus was leaning forward now.

In cross-examination he didn't attack. "Your landlord analogy," he said. "Did you invent that just now, or are you stealing from Mill?" "I demur," Julia said. "I'd call it borrowing." The third judge, the one who never smiled, smiled.

She lost anyway, on a two-to-one decision, the dissenting judge citing "the only genuinely responsive rebuttal of the round." Marcus found her afterward by the water fountain. "The steel-man thing," he said. "That has a name. People do it on purpose?" "Apparently I do it on purpose now," Julia said. He turned the pages of his notes back and forth, the way he did when a book had misled him. "I still think I'm right," he said. "I know," she said. "That's the part I can't fix."

Walking out, she tried to decide whether she'd won something or merely lost more interestingly than usual. The two ways of thinking sat side by side in her, refusing to merge: Marcus's discipline of definitions and her father's mute, buried reasons, both real, both incomplete. She texted her father that she'd be home by eleven, and then, after a pause, by eleven-thirty, and put the phone in her pocket before he could answer.

story:
By the time Mr. Okonkwo called on her, Noemie had already decided she would win the debate, which was the first mistake, though she did not know it yet.

"Minimum wage," he said, writing it on the board. "Resolved: the government should raise it. Noemie and Priya, you're for. Marcus and Daniil, against. Twenty minutes of prep."

She liked this classroom better than any other, third floor, west light, the radiators that ticked like a slow clock. She and Priya dragged their desks together and Priya opened her laptop. Priya always opened her laptop. Noemie preferred the library, the weight of a book in her hands, but there was no time, so she leaned in and began listing arguments on a folded page of her notebook.

"Fifteen dollars isn't enough to live on," she said. "That's the whole case. Wages have to be a floor. That's what the law is for."

"Marcus will say small businesses close," Priya said, typing. "He read something about it last night, he told Daniil in the hallway. I heard them."

"You heard them." Noemie underlined her first point twice. She was certain she had heard nothing of the kind, but Priya's certainty had a way of becoming hers, and anyway it didn't matter, because the case was simple. Every civilized country had a legal minimum wage. That was the spine of her argument. She had learned it from her father, who had worked nights at a bakery for eleven years and who said, every time the subject came up, that without the law the owners would pay people in crumbs.

Marcus opened with the small business line, exactly as predicted, and Noemie knocked it down with a statistic about productivity she had copied from a poster in the corridor outside, a poster she was fairly sure was about productivity. The exchange was quick and clean. Daniil mumbled something about inflation. Then Marcus, shuffling his notes, said, "Here's the thing, though. You keep saying every country has one. That's actually not true."

"It is true," Noemie said.

"Denmark," Marcus said. "Norway. Sweden."

"What about them?"

"No statutory national minimum wage."

"They have one," Noemie said. "Everyone has one. It's like saying some countries don't have a minimum age for school."

Mr. Okonkwo, from the back of the room, said only, "Sources, please. Both of you."

At lunch she went to the library, because she did not lose, and because something in Marcus's voice had been flat and certain in a way that unsettled the physiology of her confidence, her hands cold on the table, her pulse sitting high in her throat. The librarian showed her the comparative labour tables in the reference section, and there it was, in a grid of countries: Denmark, no statutory national minimum wage. Norway, none. Sweden, none. The entry explained that pay floors there came through collective agreements between unions and employers. She read it three times. The countries she would have named as the best places in the world to work had built their floors out of bargaining, not out of a line in a statute.

She found Priya in the corridor. "They really don't have one. Denmark, Norway, Sweden. The floors come from collective agreements. Unions and employers."

"So we're wrong?"

"We're not wrong that there's a floor. We're wrong about where it comes from." Noemie was aware that this distinction felt enormous to her and might look like nothing to Priya, who was already scrolling her phone.

The afternoon session of the debate was where it fell apart, or came together, depending on which version Noemie later told. Marcus repeated his claim and cited the same tables, and Noemie, instead of denying it, said, "He's right about that." The room went quiet. "Denmark, Norway, Sweden, no statutory national minimum wage, that's true. But the pay floors still exist. They're set through collective agreements between unions and employers." She heard her own voice and it sounded steadier than she felt. "So it isn't law versus nothing. It's law versus organized workers."

"That helps you," Daniil said, confused. "That's still a floor."

"It complicates us," Noemie said. "Because it means the law isn't the only thing standing between workers and crumbs. My dad thinks it is. He worked nights for eleven years and he thinks without that statute the owners would grind everyone down, and maybe he's right about his bakery, and maybe a country full of strong unions would protect him a different way, and I don't know which one you can actually count on."

"That's not an argument," Priya whispered.

"It's two arguments," Noemie whispered back. "I'm holding both."

Mr. Okonkwo let the silence run a moment too long before he called time. Afterward, in the emptying room, he said, "You should be careful of the tautological version of your own case. 'Every civilized country has a minimum wage, therefore a country with one is civilized.' That proves nothing." Noemie nodded as though she had known this all along, though she had never once put it that way, even to herself.

She walked home the long way, past the bakery, closed now, its ovens cold, and tried to metabolize the afternoon. She would tell her father that the Nordic countries had no statutory national minimum wage, and she already knew how he would laugh and say, so the government just lets them fight it out, and she would say no, the unions and the employers set the floors together in agreements, and he would say, and who do you trust, a paper you sign or a law you can take to court. She did not have an answer. She stopped in front of the dark window and looked at the reflection of a girl who had won every argument she could remember, holding her notebook against her chest, and started writing, at the top of a fresh page, the words my dad says.

story:
Elijah had the microfiche room to himself on a Tuesday in June, which was the only reason he had chosen it: the air conditioning worked there, and nobody asked what a seventeen-year-old was doing alone in a library at two in the afternoon. His father had lost his job at the cannery in March, and the house had become a place of careful voices, so Elijah had started taking his college application essay anywhere else. The prompt asked him to describe an issue he had changed his mind about, and he had chosen the local paper's coverage of the cannery closing, mostly because it was the only thing he could not stop thinking about.

The essay was not going well. He had written half a page about how the paper had run four stories about the closing, all of them about stock prices and company statements, and none of them about the three hundred people his father worked beside for twenty-two years. Then he had deleted it, because it sounded like a complaint, and complaints were not essays. What he wanted was a reason the paper had written it that way, and he did not have one.

He was staring at his notebook when he heard the tapping. An old man at the next table was trying to feed a quarter into the microfilm printer and missing the slot, his hand shaking in a way that suggested the shaking was not new. Elijah watched for a moment, then walked over. "Here, let me get that." He fed the coin in, and the machine groaned and printed a grainy page from 1987. The headline was about a broadcaster.

"Thank you, son." The man turned the page toward the light. "I was looking for this. My granddaughter's doing a project, and I told her I remembered when it happened, and she said, prove it." He laughed, a dry, pleased sound. "I was a raconteur at that plant over on Fell Street, thirty years, everybody's stories, and now the only audience I can hold is her."

Elijah glanced at the page. "What happened in 1987?"

"The Fairness Doctrine. That was the rule. The FCC made broadcasters put contrasting views on the air about controversial public issues, starting in 1949." He tapped the date with one crooked finger. "And then in 1987, the FCC abolished it. Gone. I remember Dan Rather having to say goodnight to it, almost." He looked at Elijah with sudden attention. "You writing something?"

"College essay. About the paper here, how it covered the cannery closing." Elijah heard himself say it and felt the familiar embarrassment, but the old man did not laugh.

"Who owns your paper?"

"I don't know."

"Find out. That's a story too." The man gathered his printout and his granddaughter's project folder, and he said, "I'd stay and talk your ear off, but she's waiting in the car, and she honks," and he was gone before Elijah could ask his name.

The library's periodical room had a shelf of bound volumes of the local paper and, more usefully, a computer with a database of business filings. Elijah typed in the paper's name and followed it the way the reference librarian, a tired woman named Ms. Okafor who had nevertheless shown him the database without being asked twice, had taught him: parent company, then parent of the parent. The paper was owned by a group headquartered two states away, and that group was owned in part by an investment firm, and the investment firm held a stake in the company that had bought the cannery. He sat back. The words on the screen did not say the coverage was shaped by that. They only said the connection existed, quiet as plumbing behind a wall.

He went back to the microfilm. In 1975, the same paper had run a labor dispute across six issues, with union quotes on the front page. In 1994, a similar dispute got two paragraphs inside, both from management. It was not proof of anything; he knew that, the way he knew a lot of things he could not yet argue. But the pattern had a shape now, and the shape had a history, and the history had a date.

He found Ms. Okafor reshelving near the window and asked whether a newspaper was bound by the Fairness Doctrine, since it was about broadcasters. She said she thought it applied to radio and television licenses, not print, and that he should verify that himself rather than trust her memory. He did, in an old media law textbook with a cracked spine, and she was right, which made the essay harder and truer. The doctrine was gone, and even when it had lived, it had never circumscribed what his paper could print. Its absence explained the air; it did not explain the weather.

He wrote until five, then read it over. The essay said what he had found, and then it said what he had not: that ownership could shape coverage, that he had watched it lean, and that he could not prove the lean was directed by anyone at all. He thought about his father reading it, if his father ever did, and he left in the part about the three hundred workers, because they were the reason, and he cut the part where he had called the paper's editors cowards, because it was trenchant and it was also cheap, and the old man's voice was in his head saying that a story was not the same as a swing.

He saved the file twice, the way his father had taught him, and copied it to a drive for the drive's own sake. On his way out he saw the old man's granddaughter's project folder still on the microfiche table, left behind, a pencil tucked in the fold. He picked it up and carried it to the front desk. "Somebody was using the machine in the back," he said. "An older man, with a laugh you could hear across the room. He'll come back for this."

Ms. Okafor took the folder and set it where lost things went, next to a pair of reading glasses and somebody's house keys. "He will," she said. "They always come back. It's the ones with unfinished business."

"Then he's safe," Elijah said, and pushed through the doors into the heat.

story:
The argument began over a worksheet, of all things. Mr. Okafor had set out photocopies of Roman sources on the long tables, inscriptions and coin rubbings and a page of excerpted letters, and asked each pair to decide what the sources could tell them about ordinary lives. Dev, who sat beside Faith only because the seating chart said so, pushed the page away after a minute. "This is all men," he said. "Soldiers, governors, emperors. Ancient women left no voice. There's nothing to analyze."

Faith said nothing, but she copied the sentence into her notebook with a line under it. She had spent the summer reading about Roman Britain for a project she had since abandoned, and she had a feeling, half memory and half stubbornness, that Dev was wrong. The problem was that she could not yet say how. At lunch she went to the library and asked for the shelf on Roman Britain, and the librarian, without a word, pointed her toward the dusty end where nobody went.

She found the Vindolanda tablets in a thick illustrated book, thin leaves of wood photographed against black velvet, the writing faded to the color of weak tea. One tablet was a birthday party invitation, written around 100 CE, from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, the wife of a commander at the fort. Claudia wished her sister a happy birthday, promised a cheerful day, and asked her to come. It was domestic, ordinary, almost boring. Faith read the catalog entry twice, and then a third time, because of the last sentence. The closing lines were believed to be among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman. She photocopied the page with hands that were not quite steady.

The next morning the classroom was cold, its north windows giving off a thin, boreal light that lay in pale bars across the tables. When Mr. Okafor opened the floor for findings, Faith put up her hand before Dev could speak. "Yesterday someone said ancient women left no voice," she said, and held up the photocopy. "This is a birthday invitation. Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, around 100 CE, from the fort at Vindolanda. And the closing lines are some of the earliest known Latin we have written by a woman."

"Written by a woman," Dev said. "Or written for one."

"That's not what it says."

"That's what it means." He had turned in his seat, arms folded. "Roman elites had scribes. Her husband commanded a fort. Somebody else held the pen."

Faith had expected him to fold, and he had not, and she felt the ground shift under her nice neat discovery. Mr. Okafor, who had a habit of stepping back when students fought, wrote two dates on the board and said only, "Two textbooks disagree about that tablet. See which ones." So the class split the sources between them, and for twenty minutes the room was all shuffling and low argument.

The disagreement was real and it was not polite. One book, published in the 1990s, treated the invitation as a treasure and moved on. A second, more recent, discussed the closing lines in detail, noting that most of the tablet appeared to be in a professional hand. A third article, dense and hedged, argued about what counted as evidence at all. Faith read with her chin on her fist, drifting once into a reverie of Claudia at some northern birthday table, candles or lamplight, snow maybe, and then jerked back because Priya across the table was holding out the second book, tapping a paragraph.

"Here," Priya said. "The bulk of the letter looks like a scribe's work. But the closing lines are different."

"Different how?"

"Read it."

Faith read. The editors themselves did not agree, and she understood, slowly, that they could not, because the sources were partial and the questions kept changing. The tablet was one small wooden leaf. The historians were not looking at different tablets; they were looking at the same faded scratches and asking different things of them. One asked whether a woman could write. Another asked whether a woman's words could survive a scribe's hand. Neither question absolved the other of being a real question.

When the class reassembled, Mr. Okafor asked for conclusions. Dev went first and said the invitation was probably dictated, that the evidence was ambiguous. Faith stood with the photocopy and did not say he was wrong. "I brought this to prove you wrong," she said. "It doesn't, not completely. The closing lines are what we have, and they're some of the earliest known Latin writing by a woman, and nobody can prove whose hand made them. That's the whole thing. That's all we get."

"That's not much," Dev said.

"It's a birthday party," Faith said. "She wanted her friend to come. That's more than nothing." She set the photocopy down on the table between them, the two faded columns of ink faceup, and slid it across to his side.

story:
The acceptance email arrived at 4:47 on a Tuesday afternoon, while Alexa was supposed to be taking notes on the Missouri Compromise. Her phone sat face-down on her desk, as required, but it buzzed twice against the laminate, and she knew before she looked. She asked for the bathroom pass with a steadiness that surprised her, walked down the empty hallway with its smell of floor wax and boiled pasta, and stood in the last stall of the second-floor bathroom reading the words on a screen the size of her palm. Congratulations. We are pleased. She read it four times, and each time the sentence seemed to belong to a different person.

By Wednesday morning, half the senior class knew. Priya cornered her at the lockers before first period, breathless, insisting Alexa was done, finished, set. "You got in," Priya said. "Why would you keep writing essays for other schools? It's over."

"It's Early Action," Alexa said. "It gives you an early decision, but it's non-binding. I could still choose not to go."

Priya waved this away like smoke. "You're going to go."

That was the sentence that followed Alexa through the day, into sixth period, into Mr. Delgado's classroom with its radiator that clanked like a coin in a tin cup and its windows fogged from the December cold. The regular deadline for most of her other applications was January first, which meant she had twelve days to decide whether to finish five more essays or let them die quietly in her college portal. Mr. Delgado had given the class a work period for their term papers, and Alexa sat in the back row with her laptop open to a document titled "Why Northwestern," a document that was 212 words long and had been 212 words long for two weeks.

Derek sat diagonal from her, morose as always in December, hood up, thumbing through a printout of a rejection letter he'd received the same afternoon. He had applied Early Decision somewhere and been denied, and he wore it now the way other people wore a cast. "At least you got good news," he said, not looking up. "You can coast until June. I have to start over."

"It's not binding," Alexa said again, quieter this time, and heard how the words sounded less like freedom and more like an obligation she hadn't finished paying. Derek looked at her then, and something in his face, envy maybe, or simple exhaustion, made her feel the weight of what she was holding. She had an answer. She had wanted an answer for two years, had postulated since freshman year that an acceptance would settle everything, that the moment the email came, the anxious machinery in her chest would finally stop.

The machinery had not stopped. It had, if anything, found new work.

She typed a sentence about Northwestern's journalism program and deleted it. The radiator clanked. Someone near the front was eating an orange, and the citrus smell cut through the stuffy heat, sharp and specific, and she thought suddenly of her mother peeling oranges on the porch last summer, saying, you'll go where you go, it doesn't matter to me, which Alexa had understood even then to be a kind of lie, a generous one. Her mother wanted the big school, the famous one, the one whose name made people at church nod. The school that had accepted her was good but not famous. The school she had 212 words about was both.

Priya slid into the seat beside her, having abandoned her own term paper. "You're still writing it," she said, almost accusing. "I can't believe you're still writing it."

"I don't know what I'm doing," Alexa said. "That's the honest answer. I have one yes in my hand and I don't know if it's the right yes, and if I stop now, I'll never find out what the other answers would have been."

"So apply everywhere. Keep all the doors open. What's the problem?"

"The problem is I've been beguiling myself for two years that one letter would make the decision for me. It doesn't. It just moves the decision to December instead of April."

Priya was quiet for a moment, chewing on this. "That's still a better problem than Derek's."

Alexa glanced at Derek, at the rejection letter now folded into a small square on his desk, at his hood, at the window behind him where the fog was thick enough to draw in. She picked up her finger and drew a letter A, then wiped it away with her sleeve, because it felt like claiming something she hadn't claimed yet.

"What's the essay about?" Priya asked.

"Supposedly, why I want to go there."

"And why do you?"

Alexa looked at the 212 words on her screen. They were true words, careful words, and they had nothing in them she could point to and call a reason. She set her hands on the keyboard. "Give me until the deadline," she said. "Twelve days. Then I'll tell you both of us."

Mr. Delgado rapped his knuckles on his desk and announced twenty minutes left in the period, and the orange smell reached the back row, and Alexa began to type.

story:
The hardware store smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and Ava stood at the register of Korner Supply on a Tuesday morning in June, filling out the last form between her and an apron. She had already written her name twice, once in her careful hand and once in her rushing hand, and both looked like they belonged to someone younger. The form was called a W-4, the manager had said, sliding it across the counter with a pen that had a chewed cap, and now she was staring at a box that wanted to know something she did not understand at all.

"It tells me how much to withhold," she said slowly, reading the top line to herself. The words were English, each one individually familiar, but the sentence had the texture of a riddle. She gathered that the federal income tax was involved, and that each paycheck was involved, and that her answers would somehow connect the two, but the connecting logic was not on the page. Her mother would know. Her mother did the family taxes every April with a shoebox of receipts and a specific facial expression that Ava had learned not to interrupt.

She took out her phone and typed, "At the job. They gave me a form. W-4? Do you know what this is." Then she reconsidered the question mark, kept it anyway, and sent it. The manager, a broad man named Dale who wore his reading glasses on a cord around his neck, was unpacking a box of tape measures two aisles over, and she could hear him counting under his breath, forty-one, forty-two, as though the tape measures might disobey him.

Her phone buzzed. "Withholding. You fill out the W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck." Ava read the text twice. So the form was not a tax itself; it was a piece of information she handed over, and the store used it to do the taking-out. That felt manageable, almost polite, like telling someone in advance how you took your coffee. She filled in the lines her mother walked her through by text, one slow reply at a time, while a customer waited behind her to buy a single bolt.

"First job?" the customer asked. He was holding the bolt in his fist like evidence.

"Is it obvious?"

"You're apologizing to the pen," he said, and paid for his bolt and left.

Dale put her on paint for the first week, which suited her, because the paint aisle had a fan and because the names of the colors were their own small literature. There was a chip called Littoral Gray, a soft blue-green, and when a woman came in asking for something to remind her of the shore, Ava turned the fan deck to that one without having to look it up. "It's a coastal kind of color," she said, and the woman held it up to the light and said it was exactly the water at her grandmother's house in Maine, and bought two gallons.

The work had a substrate of repetition under everything else, she decided by Thursday: unlocking, sweeping, restocking, the register's little songs. But things kept surfacing through it. A man came in wanting to repaint his front door in a way that would, he admitted, "aggrandize the whole entryway," and Ava had not known that a door could be aggrandized, though she recognized the impulse, having spent a fair portion of her own energy on being perceived favorably. He chose a deep red. She mixed it on the shaker machine, which sounded like a small rebellion, and thought about how much of wanting to be seen was like paint, a coat you applied over whatever the door actually was.

The paycheck arrived on the fifteenth, in an envelope with her name typed on it, and it was smaller than the number she had computed in her head on the bus. She stood at the time clock doing the subtraction again, then looked at the stub, where a line item said FED INCOME TAX, and the riddle from her first morning assembled itself into sense. She had marked that box, and the store had done exactly what she told it to. It occurred to her that she had made a real decision, with consequences, at a moment when she felt entirely ignorant, and that the decision had worked anyway, more or less, the way most of her decisions seemed to. She could not decide whether that was reassuring or slightly frightening, and she suspected it was both, and that the two feelings were going to coexist for a while.

She texted her mother a photo of the stub. Her mother replied with a single thumbs-up, which Ava interpreted as pride filtered through whatever the parental equivalent of a W-4 was, some withholding of its own.

At closing, Dale asked how the first paycheck felt. Ava considered saying smaller than expected, or educational, or fine, and chose the truest available option.

"Like I told a form something and it listened," she said. Dale laughed once, a short bark, and handed her the keys to lock the paint aisle gate.

"You'll get faster at that bolt drawer," he said, and turned off the lights over the registers, one switch at a time, while the tape measures hung in their rows, waiting for morning.
