story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic and floor cleaner, and Emile stood at the counter holding his mother's old phone, the one with the crack running diagonally across the screen like a fault line on a map. His own phone had died three weeks ago, and he had a summer job starting Monday at the landscaping company, which meant he needed something that worked, today, before he had the money to pay for it outright.

The sales rep, a woman named Dana with a lanyard and the patient gravitas of someone who had explained the same forms a thousand times, turned a tablet toward him. "You can put it on a payment plan," she said. "Twenty-two a month for twenty-four months." Emile did the arithmetic in his head and felt something tighten. Twenty-two times twenty-four was five hundred twenty-eight. The phone's price tag said four hundred ninety-nine.

"So it costs more this way," he said. "Twenty-nine dollars more." Dana nodded without apology. "That's the interest," she said. "That's what borrowing costs. You're paying for the use of money you don't have yet." He looked at the tablet, at his own signature half-formed in the signature box, and thought about how the number was small enough to seem like nothing and large enough to be real.

Then Dana ran his information and paused. "There's a late payment here from March," she said. "Looks like a phone bill. It's showing on your credit." Emile's stomach dropped. He remembered it exactly: the app, the notification he'd swiped away during a chemistry study session, the bill that had slipped his mind for six weeks during track season. "How bad is that?" he asked. "Like, does one missed bill ruin everything?"

Dana turned the screen so he could see the breakdown. "Payment history is the largest factor in your FICO score," she said. "About thirty-five percent of it, for the general population." He read the numbers on the screen and understood, slowly, that the forgotten bill he had treated as nothing had touched the single biggest thing a lender would look at. Not all of it, not close, but the largest piece. "It fades," Dana added. "It's not forever. But it's there."

He signed, because Monday was coming and the job was real, and then he sat on the bench near the accessories wall while the transfer ran. Two college guys stood at the next counter, arguing in the easy, half-joking way of people who had read one article and become doctrinaire about it. "Credit's a trap," one said. "They design it to vilify the poor and forgive the rich." The other shook his head. "It's a tool. If you pay on time it works for you. My sister's score got her an apartment." They went back and forth, and Emile found himself unable to agree with either of them completely.

He thought about the twenty-nine dollars, about how the same force that took money from him when he borrowed could give money to him if he saved, because Dana had mentioned it offhand while ringing him up: his bank paid interest on savings, small but real, money earning money while he slept. Two directions of the same principle. He had missed a payment and that mistake would follow him, but it was thirty-five percent, not one hundred percent; the rest was still his to shape, starting with the twenty-two dollars due each month, which he now intended to automate so that neither track season nor chemistry nor anything else could swallow it again.

At home he set up the autopay and then, after a minute, moved forty dollars from checking into the savings account his mother had opened for him years ago and he had never touched. The interest rate was pitiful, something like one and a half percent, and he laughed a little at how little it would earn. Still, he watched the balance on the screen, four hundred and six dollars, and imagined it drifting upward while the phone debt drifted downward, two lines crossing somewhere in a future he couldn't quite see. His mother called from the kitchen asking if he wanted dinner. He closed the laptop and said, "Yeah, I'm coming."

story:
Victor had spent three weeks drafting his bill on later school start times, and when the model parliament convened in the drafty assembly hall of the provincial legislature, he carried the typed pages like something living. The clerk, a university student named Priya in a borrowed black robe, called the house to order. Victor stood, his throat dry, ready to argue. "Bill 12, An Act to Amend the Education Act with Respect to School Start Times," Priya read, and before he could open his mouth she had moved on to the next item. Twelve seconds, maybe less. No questions, no debate, not even a vote. Around him the other students exchanged looks of pure bewilderment, and a girl named Marta whispered, "That was it? That was nothing."

At the lunch break Victor found Priya stacking the order paper and asked her whether his bill had been disqualified somehow, whether he had filled out a form wrong. She laughed, not unkindly. "That's first reading," she said. "In the real UK Parliament, a government bill's first reading is a formality. It just gets introduced, no debate, no vote." Victor stared at her, feeling oddly cheated. He had imagined the moment his idea entered the world as a public battle, not a name read into a record. "So it doesn't mean anything?" he asked. "It means it exists now," Priya said, and went back to her papers.

The committee stage came after lunch, and that was where the bleeding began. Victor had written a clause mandating a nine o'clock start for all high schools in the fictional province. A delegate from the rural party, a broad-shouldered boy named Ellis, moved an amendment allowing boards to opt out for bus scheduling reasons. Victor argued that an opt-out clause was a hole you could drive a bus through, and the room laughed, but the amendment carried anyway, eleven votes to nine. In the hallway afterward Ellis found him at the water fountain and offered something like an armistice: rural boards would accept the bill if they could breathe, and without rural boards, there would be no bill at all. Victor said he would think about it, which was true, and that it was a betrayal, which he also believed.

He thought about it through the debate that evening, sitting in the back benches while other bills rose and fell. A delegate proposing free menstrual products in schools watched her bill die at second reading on a voice vote, the "noes" rolling through the chamber like weather. Victor noticed that she did not cry, though her jaw worked. He noticed, too, that she was back at her desk within the hour, annotating a new draft in green ink. His friend Dev, slouched beside him, called this congenital optimism, the kind you were born with, and Victor envied it even as he distrusted it. Dev himself had come to the weekend to lose bills, he said, the way other people went to the gym.

What Victor worked out, slowly, in the yellow light of the chamber, was that two things he had been treating as one were actually two. He had wanted the law, and he had wanted to be right, and the committee had forced him to see that the second could cost him the first. He didn't think the trade was fair. He didn't think it was clean. But when debate on his own bill opened after dinner, he rose on a point of order and announced, to his own surprise, that he would accept the amendment as drafted. Marta, who had voted for the opt-out, looked at him strangely, almost disappointed, as though he had surrendered something she had wanted to watch him defend.

The third reading was almost quiet after that. Members who had fought him in committee now spoke of the bill as sensible, balanced, the kind of word that used to mean something before it meant nothing. The vote was called, and Victor watched the clerk tally the standing bodies in the aisles. Twenty-two for, seven against. A majority, an ordinary miracle, accomplished without anyone changing their mind about anything except him. Priya declared the bill passed, and the house moved on to the next order of business before his pulse had slowed.

The closing ceremony simulated royal assent. The Speaker, an actual retired MLA who had agreed to attend, sat beneath the carved provincial crest and read the titles of the bills that had survived the weekend, Victor's among them, in a flat ceremonial voice. "The bill receives assent and is now law," she said, and there was a small smattering of applause, mostly from parents who had drifted in for the last hour. Victor stood with the others while the Sergeant-at-Arms carried the mace out of the chamber, the old brass catching the light, the whole thing over.

Outside, in the parking lot, the evening had gone cold and the real buses were already idling. Ellis was loading a duffel bag into a minivan. "Your law's got a hole in it," he called across the asphalt. Victor shrugged into his jacket. "So does every law," he said. "I read the rest of the order paper." Ellis grinned and shut the van door, and Victor stood a moment longer listening to the engines.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
story:
The summer research slot came down to one afternoon in the optics lab, and Makayla had planned for it the way she planned for exams, which was to say too much and then sleep badly. Forty seniors from her school were rotating through the university's physics building in groups of six. Her group had drawn the spectroscopy bench on the third floor, where a graduate student named Corinne handed each of them a printed card and told them to record what they saw through the eyepiece.

Priya went first. She looked for a long time and wrote "faint dark lines, maybe three, hard to say." Then Corinne tapped the card and said, "For this demo, you're looking for bright emission lines in the green region. Four of them." Priya leaned back in, and within thirty seconds her pencil was moving. "Oh, yeah," she said. "Four. They're right there. I don't know how I missed it."

Makayla kept her eyes on the bench while the other four took their turns. Every one of them saw four lines after being told to expect four. When her turn came, she looked before Corinne said anything to her, and she saw what Priya had seen at first: dark lines, indistinct, count uncertain. She wrote that down. Corinne read it, then read it again.

"Interesting," Corinne said. "You're the only one who recorded dark lines."

"I wrote it before you told me what to look for," Makayla said. "Does that matter?"

Corinne didn't answer directly. She pulled a stool over and sat, which the other grad students in the room did not do. "Have you heard of René Blondlot?" she asked the group. Nobody had. "A French physicist, claimed to discover a new kind of radiation. He called them N-rays."

"Like X-rays," said Dario, the boy next to Makayla.

"Right. In 1904 another physicist, Robert W. Wood, went to Blondlot's lab and secretly removed a key prism from the apparatus. The observers still reported seeing the N-rays." Corinne stood up and straightened the eyepiece. "Wood didn't announce what he'd done until after. That's the part people remember."

Makayla turned her card over. On the back, in the margin, she had written her prep notes that morning, half of them definitions she'd exhumed from an old textbook in the school library, because the research program's application asked for a short essay on "how we know what we know." One of the notes said logos, from her English class, argument that persuades by reason. She had underlined it twice. Now the word looked thin to her, like it assumed reason was a thing one person could hold whole in one hand.

"Is this demo rigged, then?" Priya asked. There was an edge in her voice, and Makayla understood it. Priya had already emailed the program coordinator saying the lab visit confirmed her interest in optics.

"It's not rigged," Corinne said. "The lamp is exactly what I said it is. The question is what a single observer is worth."

Makayla thought about that on the walk to the next station, and she thought about it through the boring part of the tour, the clean room with its yellow light, and the part where Dario asked whether the university had ever retracted a paper. One result wasn't anything, she'd known that in an abstract way, but she hadn't felt it until Priya's pencil started moving. Still, she wasn't sure the feeling was fair. Priya wasn't lying. Corinne's tip about the green lines was presumably true, and Priya's second look was presumably better than her first. Expectation could point you at something real. The problem was that the pointing and the seeing felt identical from the inside, and only one of them counted as evidence.

At the bus turnaround she caught up with Corinne, who was carrying a crate of extension cords to a van. Makayla said she wanted to apply for the slot and asked, since it would come up in the essay, whether Corinne thought a study should be thrown out when the observers knew what they expected.

"One observer, one afternoon? That was never a study," Corinne said. She shifted the crate to her hip. "You'd repeat it, other people would repeat it with different instruments, people who wanted you to be wrong would repeat it. Then you'd know something."

"Unless they were all expecting the same thing," Makayla said.

"Then it takes longer," Corinne said. She loaded the crate and shut the van door.

On the bus Makayla wrote two sentences in her notebook and crossed out the second one, which had claimed too much. The first said that she had seen dark lines and had no way, from inside her own head, to certify them, and that the certification would have to come from outside her, repeatedly, from people with no stake in what she'd written. She looked at Priya two rows up, headphones in, filling out the program's online form on her phone. Priya typed fast, and stopped once, and looked out the window at the loading dock, and then typed again.

story:
The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Nicholas had been rehearsing in the hallway long enough to notice both. He held his outline flat against a binder, the way he had seen lawyers do it in videos, and read the first line of his argument under his breath. In forty minutes he would stand before a panel of three judges in a borrowed courtroom and argue the student's side of Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., the case his civics class had drawn by lottery. Then, after lunch, he would argue the school's side of the same case, which was the part nobody had warned him would be hard.

He had not chosen the case. Priya had pulled the slip from the coffee can and read the name aloud, and Marcus, who sat behind him, had laughed and said it sounded like a school board suing a letter. Nicholas had gone home that weekend and looked it up, partly for the assignment and partly because of something he had posted in March, a picture of his cross country coach with a caption he had deleted by Sunday but which three people had screenshotted. Nothing had come of it. Still, when he read the summary of the case, he felt the specific cold of recognition.

The case was about a girl who had posted something on Snapchat, off campus, on a weekend, and her school had punished her for it. Nicholas had assumed, before he read further, that the school was allowed to do that, that off campus was like a country the school's rules didn't reach but its arm did. Then he found the holding. In 2021, the Supreme Court had ruled 8 to 1 that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Eight justices against one. He read the sentence twice, then copied it onto an index card, because it seemed like the kind of thing that shouldn't be paraphrased.

The courtroom was crepuscular in the late morning, the blinds tilted so that light fell in gray bars across the jury box, which sat empty. A bailiff who was actually a retired accountant let them in and told them not to touch the microphone. Nicholas took the petitioner's table, the one closest to the bench, and arranged his cards in order while Priya sat beside him with the case brief and a bag of pretzels she did not open. At the respondent's table, two juniors Nicholas didn't know well spread out their notes like a poker hand they were proud of.

"Ms. Reyes, you may begin whenever you're ready," said the judge in the center, a law student named Alanna who wore her father's old robe. Nicholas stood. His first two minutes went fine, better than fine; he talked about the post being made off campus, on her own time, and he said the line from his index card almost exactly, that the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 1 in 2021 that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Alanna nodded and wrote something down, and the nod coagulated all his scattered preparation into something that felt like actual confidence.

Then the judge on the left leaned forward. "Counsel, what would you say to the school if the post had disrupted a class on Monday?" It was the question Nicholas had hoped wouldn't come, because he had two answers and they disagreed with each other. He gave the student's answer first, that punishment for a weekend post stretches the school's reach into students' private lives. Then he stopped, because the honest thing was also true. "And I'd have to concede that schools aren't helpless," he said. "I just don't think the First Amendment turns off when a student walks through her front door."

At lunch, in the courthouse cafeteria, Marcus slid his tray across from Nicholas and asked how it had gone. "I don't know yet," Nicholas said. "Ask me after round two." The problem was the second round. For an hour he had believed the student's side so completely that he could feel it in his chest, and now he had to stand up and be the school, the district that had suspended a girl for swearing on a weekend. He spread his cards on the table and tried to see the other argument, but his thoughts kept sliding back, the way a whole biome shifts when one species is removed; the case without the student's rights in it wasn't the same case at all.

When the afternoon session began, the light had moved and the courtroom was warmer. Nicholas stood at the respondent's table and argued that a school could still act when off-campus speech bled into school life, that the majority had left the door open, that the lone dissenter had a point about schools needing to reach students wherever they were. He did not fully believe it, but he argued it carefully, and once, when Alanna asked whether a school should follow students home, he heard himself say, "Not home. But maybe the bus stop in between." It was the first thing all day that felt like his own.

The panel conferred, then awarded the round to the other side, and Priya squeezed his shoulder on the way out. In the hallway, the light through the high windows had gone amber, and Nicholas stopped by the water fountain and took a long drink. He still didn't know where the line was, exactly, between a school's reach and a student's life, and he suspected the Court didn't either, given eight votes on one side and a single stubborn voice on the other. He put his index cards back in order, both sets, one for each side, and slid them into his back pocket. "Same time next week," Priya said, holding the door.

story:
The marble corridor outside Courtroom 4B smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Sophia's note cards kept slipping against her skirt. Fourteen students from three high schools had been assigned to litigate a mock case before a panel of real appellate judges, and Sophia had drawn the worst possible job: she would argue both sides. Petitioners in the morning, respondents after lunch, same girl, same bench, same fifteen minutes each.

The case was one her class had built from a real fight at a school two districts over. A student named in the file only as M.R. had posted a video mocking the vice principal, and the school had suspended her. That part was settled law, more or less. The twist her classmates had added was this: M.R. had also been banned from a private class-discussion website run by a company, and she claimed that ban violated her free speech rights too. Sophia had to argue that it did. Then, after lunch, she had to argue that it didn't.

In the morning she stood at the podium with her knees locked and said what she had prepared. She talked about the marketplace of ideas, about chilling expression, about a sixteen-year-old silenced in the very forum where her classmates gathered. Justice Kowalski, a heavyset man with reading glasses pushed low, leaned forward and asked whether the website was run by the government. Sophia said no, and he asked the question again, slower, the way you repeat something to someone who hasn't understood it the first time.

"Then walk me through it," he said. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech. It does not by itself stop a private company from restricting speech. So what is your claim?"

Her argument dissolved in her mouth. She had known the words, of course, had copied them into her outline weeks ago, but she had never actually believed them until a judge made her stand there and look at them. She said something about students feeling that the platform was their town square, and the judge said feelings did not create jurisdiction, and a girl from the other school, a redhead named Priya who'd spent the whole morning smirking, whispered something to her co-counsel that Sophia pretended not to notice.

At lunch she sat alone on the courthouse steps and ate half a sandwich. Her grandmother had once been fired from a print shop for union organizing, and the family still argued about it at holidays, her uncle insisting it was illegal, her mother correcting him each time with visible exhaustion. Sophia had always assumed her mother was being pedantic. Now she understood her mother had been protecting the family from a confusion that would cost them something later, the way you teach a kid not to touch a stove. The government couldn't punish you for speaking. A private company could, mostly, and you had to know which one you were standing in front of.

But the afternoon side was not as easy as the morning side had been hard. Arguing that M.R.'s ban was lawful felt like handing a weapon to whoever owned the forum, and the forum was where everyone her age actually lived. She stood up after lunch and made the legal argument cleanly, almost coldly, and then Justice Alvarez, a small woman with silver hair, asked the counterpoint Sophia had been dreading: "Counsel, is there anything you find troubling about the rule you're defending?" Sophia paused, and then said yes, that the law drew a line between public power and private power at a moment when private platforms felt more like governments than governments did, and that the doctrine struck her as accurate and antiquated at once, which was not a distinction the First Amendment itself could resolve.

Justice Alvarez wrote something down. Priya, sitting in the second row, was not smirking anymore.

When the judges retired to score the round, Priya came over. "The morning," she said. "When you folded on the private website. You knew, right? I could tell you knew." Sophia admitted she had known and hoped the judges wouldn't press it, and Priya laughed, a real laugh, not a smirk. "I got that exact question wrong at a tournament in October. I claimed a platform violated a girl's free speech rights and a judge spent ten minutes dismantling me. I only challenged you today to see if you'd do the same thing I did."

They were still on the steps when the clerk came out with the results folded in half. Priya took the paper, looked at it a long moment, and held it out without saying anything.

story:
Rose found the notice taped to the circulation desk of the public library, between a flyer for toddler story hour and a laminated map of the county bus routes. First-time volunteers welcome, it said, Saturday, seven a.m., dress for mud. She had been meaning to do something that wasn't school, something that would look less like a line on an application and more like a fact about her, and she had been circumspect about which something, because she distrusted her own motives and didn't want to be the girl who photographed her own kindness. She copied the address onto the back of a receipt and checked out a novel she would not read.

Saturday came cold and clear. The food bank's van waited in the library parking lot, which served as the meeting point, and beside it stood a man in a canvas jacket counting heads on a clipboard. Eleven volunteers, most of them older than Rose, all of them strangers. The man, whose name was Teodoro, drove them out past the edge of town to a farm where the squash field had already been picked over once by the crew that mattered, the paid crew, the main harvest.

"You'll see squash out there still," Teodoro said as they stepped down into the rows. "Anything you gather goes to the food bank. It's called gleaning." He said it the way he might have said the word for a bird or a tool, and then he handed out crates and gloves and walked off toward the far end of the field.

The rows were messy in a way Rose hadn't expected. The plants lay half flattened, and under them the squash had gone pale where the ground had touched them, scarred where a machine had brushed past. She picked one up, turned it over, and hesitated over a soft brown patch the size of her thumb. Whole or not whole. She looked up to ask someone and saw that the other volunteers had already scattered, bent and working, their crates filling without ceremony. Nobody was going to tell her. She set the blemished one aside and kept the rest.

Dana, the volunteer nearest her, was maybe sixty and moved with the ease of a person who had done this many seasons. "Soft spots mean it won't store," Dana said, not looking up. "Hard ones are just ugly. People think food bank means perfect produce, and then it rots in the field because nobody paid for it." Rose asked whether the farmer couldn't sell it, and Dana shrugged one shoulder. "After the main harvest, what's left isn't worth the labor to him. But it's still food. So we come." Rose worked that around while she worked the row. It seemed to her a strange economy, that a thing could be worthless and good at the same time, and she tested the idea against each squash she lifted.

By mid-morning the problem found them. The crates were full, more than half the field still unpicked, and the van had room for only what was crated. The second shift, Teodoro announced from the end of the row, had fallen through, so whatever they didn't get today would be disked into the soil on Monday. Rose watched the volunteers glance at each other, at the sun, at their phones. One by one they began to say they had things, errands, a granddaughter's recital. Teodoro didn't argue. He began stacking crates with the flat efficiency of a man preparing to lose.

Rose had been quiet all morning, and quiet people can sometimes say a thing plainly. "We don't all have to stay," she said. "Some of us could keep picking while the van runs the first load over. Then it comes back for the rest." Dana looked at her, then at the field, then at Teodoro. Teodoro turned his clipboard over as if the answer might be written on the back.

From where Dana stood, it looked like this: a girl of eighteen, mud to the knees of a jacket too thin for the weather, holding a scarred squash in both hands like evidence in a case she was still arguing with herself. Dana had spent enough years in this work to know that schemes hatched at eleven in the morning often died by noon, and she was not going to flatter the girl by pretending otherwise. But she had also spent enough years to know that a full crate driven to the pantry at noon fed someone at six. "I'll stay for the second round," Dana said. "I've got nothing until four." Two of the recital people, cajoled less by Teodoro than by their own shame, muttered that they could stay an hour, and the numbers on the clipboard stopped being a countdown.

The van went loaded and came back empty in time for lunch. Rose's arms ached in a way that felt specific, one muscle for lifting and another for bending, and she had learned that a soft spot was a judgment and an ugly skin was nothing at all. She still wasn't sure, when she thought about the morning, whether she had done a good thing or a merely sensible one, or whether there was a difference, and she decided she would have to come back another Saturday to find out. She stood at the tailgate stacking the last crates, and Dana handed her a squash with a long green scar down its side. "Perfect," Dana said.

story:
Jacob checked the mailbox at 4:15, the way he had every afternoon for nine days, though the mail never came before five. The box was empty except for a coupon circular and a water bill, and he stood there holding the little door open as if another letter might materialize behind the first one. His father had installed the mailbox at the edge of the gravel drive fifteen years ago, sinking the post in concrete, and over time the ground around it had turned friable, so that the whole thing listed toward the road like a man listening for something. Jacob straightened it every so often without thinking. Today he held it upright while he counted the days left before the state university's reply deadline, which was not really a deadline at all, just the last day he could say yes.

The letter, when it came, would be the fourth. Two colleges had already said no, and one had said yes but wanted thirty-eight thousand dollars a year, a figure he had read aloud to his mother and then never mentioned again. The state university was the one he could actually pay for, more or less, which was why his older sister, Dani, had taken over the kitchen table for the past three nights.

He could see her through the window when he came back up the drive, hunched at the laptop with their mother beside her, both of them lit by the screen in the dark kitchen. They were filling out the FAFSA, the form for federal financial aid, and Dani kept explaining it to him in fragments whenever he passed through. "It's how you get the Pell Grant," she said once, not looking up. "Federal money you don't pay back. And federal loans, the ones with the better rates." Another night she added, quieter, "It's not just the federal government. The state uses it too, and the colleges themselves. Almost everybody bases their aid on this one form." Their mother typed the tax numbers with one finger, then two, then asked Dani to read the line back. The state's aid deadline was tomorrow at midnight, and Dani wanted her own answer, a transfer out of the community college and into the nursing program, and that want was tangled up in the same form, the same numbers, the same parents' income.

Jacob had spent the whole application season telling anyone who asked that it was simple math. You ranked the schools, you weighed the costs, you picked the highest expected value. He called it rationalism, half as a joke, when his uncle asked at Christmas how he was choosing. But the math kept refusing to stay simple. The yes for thirty-eight thousand sat in his desk drawer, and every time he opened the drawer for a pencil he felt the weight of it, and he could not make it into a number that behaved. He wanted the big school the way you want a person, which was to say irrationally, and he wanted to be the kind of person who didn't want things that way.

On the ninth night, near eleven, Dani called him into the kitchen. "Read this," she said, and turned the laptop toward him. The form wanted to know whether their parents had filed a joint return, and then it wanted a figure from line something of that return, and their mother had gone to bed with a headache, leaving the question half answered and the deadline two hours off. Jacob found the return in the filing cabinet himself, his hands steady in a way his stomach was not, and read the number while Dani typed it. "So the aid just follows from this?" he asked. "One form, all of it?" "Federal, state, the schools' own money," Dani said. "It all starts here." She hit submit at 11:41 and then sat back and put her hands over her face, and Jacob stood there awkwardly until she said, through her fingers, "Go check the mail. Just in case."

There was nothing, of course. But he stood at the box in the cold anyway, and it was there, with the post leaning against his palm, that he understood something he could not have put in an essay. The form Dani had just filed was a machine for turning one family's circumstances into money, and the machine did not care what he deserved or what he dreamed. That should have made him feel reduced. Instead it felt almost like being absolved. The choice had never been only his; it had been made partly by tax returns and deadlines and whatever Pell Grants added up to, and he could stop treating the wanting as a personal failing.

He came back in and found Dani at the sink, drinking water, the kitchen dark again except the light over the stove. "I decided something," he said. "If the state school takes me, I'm going. The thirty-eight thousand one, I'm letting it go." Dani set down the glass. "Last week you said it was worth the debt if you got in." "Last week I was doing math with feelings and pretending they were numbers," he said. She laughed, a short surprised sound, and then grew serious. "Then maybe I can stop feeling guilty about wanting the nursing program," she said. "Mom keeps saying we can't both." Jacob shrugged. "The form says what it says. We'll see what it says."

The next afternoon he walked down the drive at 4:15 again, knowing better, and stopped anyway when he saw the white edge wedged among the coupons. The envelope was thin, which the internet said could mean anything. He carried it back to the porch steps and sat down with it unopened on his knee, and from inside the house he could hear Dani at the kitchen table, already back on the laptop, looking up the nursing program's aid page. He slid his thumb under the flap and lifted the edge, and the porch boards creaked under him as he leaned forward to read the first line.

The line outside the fire station wound past the hydrant and halfway to the hardware store, and Ella stood in it with her registration card going soft in her hand from the rain. She had forty minutes before her uncle's truck left for the airport, and the line moved in short, stubborn shuffles. Behind her, two volunteers from the Kessler campaign were arguing, not quietly, their clipboards tucked under their arms like shields.

"It's a tie," the taller one said. "Fifty-one to forty-eight, but the margin of error is four points, so it's a tie, and anyone who says otherwise is reading tea leaves."

"It's not a tie," the shorter one said. "Three points is three points."

Eella turned around. "It's within the margin of error," she said, because she had read that phrase in the newspaper on Tuesday and it had lodged in her head like a seed. The taller volunteer looked at her with something between gratitude and suspicion.

The shorter one, whose badge said DARA, shook her head. "It just means the poll can't say who's ahead," Dara said. "Not with confidence. But it doesn't mean they're exactly even." The taller volunteer, MARKUS according to his badge, opened his mouth, closed it, and then said, quietly, "That's not what the guy at the office said."

Eella had spent the drive to the fire station arguing with her own brother about exactly this, and she had lost the argument by being loud rather than right. He had said the poll was a tie; she had said Kessler was winning because the number was bigger; both of them, she understood now, had been claiming more than the number could carry. A poll was not a photograph of the whole town. It was a photograph of a few hundred people, and the margin of error was the smudge on the lens.

"Here's what I can't figure out," Markus said, and now he was talking to her directly, which she regretted and did not regret. "If we can't say Kessler's ahead, then what do we tell people at the doors? The office wants a script by noon. They want us to say the race is tied so nobody stays home."

"Say the poll can't say who's ahead," Ella said. "Say that. It's true and it's shorter than arguing about it."

Dara laughed once, a short bark, and pulled her phone out to check the time. The line moved forward three people. A man in a wet canvas coat near the door was telling anyone who would listen that all polls were lies invented by television stations, and his voice had the bombastic, carrying quality of someone who had decided volume was a form of proof. An older woman in front of Ella turned and said, "Some of us are still voting, Harold," and he subsided.

Eella checked her own phone. Thirty-one minutes. The truck was not going to wait, and her uncle was the kind of man who treated a departure time as a moral test, so missing him would debilitate her whole plan of getting to the airport and, eventually, to the college orientation she was supposed to be flying toward this afternoon. She had built her day like a row of dominoes: vote, truck, plane, new city. The line was the first domino and it refused to fall.

But she was still turning the argument over, because it was the first real thing she had gotten to think about all morning. If the lead was smaller than the margin of error, the poll was silent on the question of who was ahead. It did not say tied. It said nothing, or almost nothing, and there was a difference between nothing and an answer that people kept forgetting. Her brother would say she was splitting hairs. Maybe she was. But the polling place itself was the argument made flesh: five hundred people in a slow line, each one a number no poll had fully counted, each with the ordinary sentience of a person deciding something alone in a booth, which no sample could weigh in advance.

She turned back to the volunteers. "The script could say either candidate could be ahead," she said. "That's what the number actually supports. Then tell people to vote anyway."

Markus wrote it on the back of his flyer, the pen denting the wet paper. "Either candidate could be ahead," he repeated, as if testing whether the words would hold weight. Dara was already dialing the office. The line moved again and Ella was suddenly at the table, showing her card, printing her name in a square, receiving a sticker she pressed onto her jacket without stopping to center it.

In the booth she filled the bubble for Kessler, then stood for a moment with the pen hovering, not over doubt exactly, but over the strangeness of choosing when the numbers had refused to choose for her. She fed the ballot into the machine, heard it click, and walked out into the rain, where the truck was idling at the curb and her uncle was checking his watch.
"Doors close at noon," Markus called after her, waving the flyer. "We'll make it."

She raised a hand without turning around and ran for the passenger door.
